document.title: N=4 super Yang–Mills in Costello’s formalism — Step 1

blocks.source: 0. Overview

This manuscript constructs the one-loop quantum Batalin–Vilkovisky theory of four-dimensional \(\mathcal N=4\) super Yang–Mills theory on Euclidean \(\mathbb R^4\), together with the transformations of its local operators under the whole superconformal algebra, in the renormalization formalism of Costello [C07] and Costello–Gwilliam [CG2].

The single regulator is a lower cutoff $\varepsilon>0$ on Schwinger time, the ultraviolet (UV) boundary; the upper end of every Schwinger integral is $\infty$, so that $\varepsilon$ is the single scale of the construction.
This overview states what is constructed, where the construction needs care, how the chapters are organised, and the results of this first step.
0.1 What is constructed
The fields are those of ten-dimensional super Yang–Mills theory reduced to $\mathbb R^4$ [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], complexified.

Write $V$ for the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$ and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for the six transverse directions, and $\mathfrak g$ for the complexified gauge Lie algebra with its invariant pairing $(-,-)$, which carries the coupling.

The gauge field $A$ is a ten-component one-form with values in $\mathfrak g$: its components along $V$ form the connection $A|_V$, and its components $\iota_wA$, $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, are the six scalars.

The gaugino $\lambda$ takes values in the ten-dimensional semi-spin representation $\Sigma$, which in four dimensions is $S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*$, with $S_\pm$ the two Weyl spinor representations and $W$ the four-dimensional R-symmetry space [ESW, §10]; spinors stay index free throughout.
The ghost $c$ and the antifields $A^*$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$ complete the fields [ESW, Def 3.2, Rem 1.36].

The action $S$ is [ESW, (31)] reduced to four dimensions; its quadratic part defines the linear differential $Q$, the rest is the interaction $I$, and $\{-,-\}$ is the odd Poisson bracket [C07, Lemma 4.3.2].
Costello's construction needs three more objects.
A gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$ [C07, §1.1, Def 4.3.3], here of Feynman type, makes $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ [C07, Def 4.3.3(4)] the Laplacian on every field.
The heat kernel $K_t$ of $H$ at Schwinger time $t$ [C07, §6.5] gives the propagator
P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt ,
and Feynman graphs with these edges assemble into the renormalisation group flow of an even functional $J$,
W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J\big)=\hbar\log\Big(e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}\Big)\qquad[\text{CG2, §7.2.7}],

with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ the second-order operator contracting two fields with the kernel $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §6.4]; this is the functional called $\Gamma$ in [C07, Def 6.6.1].

As in Theorem B of [C07], whose analog on \(\mathbb R^4\) with upper scale \(\infty\) Chapter 4 proves at one loop, the counterterm \(I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\) is the singular part of the graph expansion, extracted graph by graph, with coefficients in the span of \(\varepsilon^{-1}\) and \(\log\varepsilon\) at one loop; it is local by power counting in the Schwinger times, it is unique among the translation-invariant and \(\mathfrak g\)-invariant local functionals with such coefficients, and the order-\(\hbar\) part of \(W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big)\) has a limit as \(\varepsilon\to0\), as plane-wave values at generic leg momenta.

blocks.source: A local operator $O$, for instance $\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ with $\omega$ a compactly supported four-form [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3], enters through a square-zero parameter $\delta$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.1]: the counterterm $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ of the family $I+\delta O$ defines the local operator at the UV end, $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and its quantum observable is
O[\infty]=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big)\qquad[\text{CG2, Def 8.3.1.3}].

The superconformal algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ [SW, (7), (17)] acts through an equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, a Maurer–Cartan element of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27] with differential $d_{CE}$.
Building $O[\infty]$ from the equivariant interaction, the transformation of $O$ along a generator $x_1\in\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the component $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)$.

Along the dilatation $\Delta$, the generator $2E$ of [SW, (17)] with $E$ the Euler vector field [SW, (3)], it is the anomalous dimension; along the supercharges $Q^i_\alpha$, $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha i}$ and the special supercharges $S^\alpha_i$, $\bar S^{\dot\alpha i}$ (the names of [SW, (8)]) it is the quantum-corrected supersymmetry; along the special conformal generators it is the primary condition.

blocks.source: The program therefore has two outputs: the quantized interaction, with its counterterms and its quantum master equation, and, for every local operator, its observable and its transformations along all of \(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)\).

blocks.source: The UV boundary.
The lower end $t=\varepsilon$ of the Schwinger integral carries two kernels,

\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon,\qquad (Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon,\qquad L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon\quad[\text{C07, §6.5}],
the second being [C07, Lemma 10.2.1] with $K_\infty=0$.
Edges pinned at $t=\varepsilon$ and carrying $L_\varepsilon$ produce the singular coefficients and the scaling behaviour.
Edges carrying $K_\varepsilon$ produce the defects of the quantum master equation and the transformations of observables, through

(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\big(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon\big),\qquad \Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}\quad[\text{C07, §10.1}].

Every singular or anomalous coefficient of this manuscript is carried by edges pinned at $t=\varepsilon$ and carrying $L_\varepsilon$, by special edges carrying $K_\varepsilon-K_0$, whose Schwinger time lies in $[0,\varepsilon]$, and by the counterterm vertices $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$.
0.3 Plan of the chapters
Chapter 1 fixes the fields, the odd pairing, the reduced action with its linear differential and vertices, and the classical master equation.
Chapter 2 realizes \(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)\) on Euclidean \(\mathbb R^4\) and constructs the equivariant action \(S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}\) in the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex.
Chapter 3 constructs the Feynman-gauge $Q^{GF}$, records which axioms of [C07, Def 4.3.3] it satisfies, and proves the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity at scale $\infty$ and the one-loop formula.
Chapter 4 computes the one-loop counterterms of the action in the two-, three- and four-point sectors and the quantum master equation at the UV boundary.

0.4 Results of Step 1
All one-loop coefficients are rational multiples of
\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)},
which is independent of $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ for simple $\mathfrak g$; below it is called the unit and written out in every formula.
• Chapter 2.

The equivariant action \(S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}\), with \(S^{(k)}=0\) for \(k\ge3\), satisfies its master equation for every Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\) with a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing: in arity \(0\), in arities \(\ge4\) and in arity \(3\) with at most one or with three odd arguments by a structural argument;

In arities \(1\), \(2\) and in arity \(3\) with two odd arguments by exact evaluation on every tuple of basis elements of \(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)\) for \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)\) and \(\mathfrak{su}(3)\), carried to every \(\mathfrak g\) by a color-reduction lemma.
• Chapter 3.
With the Feynman-gauge operator, $H$ is the Hodge Laplacian $d^*d+dd^*$ of flat $\mathbb R^4$, acting on every component as the positive Laplacian of functions, and
H=[Q,Q^{GF}]=d^*d+dd^*,\qquad (Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon,\qquad (Q^{GF})^2\neq0 ;
conditions (1), (2), (4) of [C07, Def 4.3.3] hold and (3), (5) fail, and every identity used later rests on the conditions that hold.

1. The classical theory

Every number computed in the following chapters is a coefficient in front of a local functional, and its sign and normalization are inherited from three classical data: the odd pairing on the fields, the BV action, and the linear differential \(Q\) [C07, §4.3].

The sources supply the ten-dimensional action [ESW, (31)] and its dimensional reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], while the pairing on the antifields stays implicit in the phrase “natural $(-1)$-shifted symplectic structure” [ESW, Def 1.34].

This chapter fixes all three data for the reduction to Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, writes the interaction vertex by vertex, and shows that the classical master equation determines the relative signs of the pairing.
1.1 Spaces and the dimensional reduction
Definition 1.1 (Spaces).

The ten-dimensional space is $V_{10}=V_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$, where $V_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^{10}$ carries its Euclidean form and the orthogonal decomposition $V_{\mathbb R}=W_{\mathbb R}\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ of [ESW, §2.2, §2.6]: $W_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^4$ is spacetime and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ consists of the six transverse directions.
With $V=W_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$,
V_{10}=V\oplus\big(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\big),
and from here on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ and $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ denote these complexifications.
The nondegenerate symmetric form $(-,-)$ of $V_{10}$ is the complex-bilinear extension of the Euclidean form.
The letter $W$ alone denotes the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10].

The gauge Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is complex, with bracket $[-,-]$ and a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing $(-,-)$ [ESW, §3.1], chosen positive definite on the compact real form, so that $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is negative definite on the real slice of [C07, §6.6] (Remark 1.10).
The coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$.
The inverse pairing is the element $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$.

The two sixteen-dimensional semi-spin representations $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^*$ of $\mathfrak{so}(V_{10})$ form the $\mathbb Z/2$-graded Clifford module $\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*$ with Clifford action $\rho$ and pairing $(-,-)\colon\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ [ESW, §2.1]:

The operator $d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $d$ for the Euclidean metric, $\mathrm{dvol}$ is the Euclidean volume density of $\mathbb R^4$, and ${\not d}=\rho\circ d$ is the Dirac operator from $\Sigma$-valued to $\Sigma^*$-valued functions [ESW, §2.1]; the same formula on $\Sigma^*$-valued functions is written ${\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}$.
The four-dimensional content of $\Sigma$ is [ESW, §10, §10.3]
\Sigma\cong S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*,\qquad \dim W=4,\qquad W\cong S_+^6\ \text{as a representation of}\ \mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)\cong SL(4,\mathbb C),
with $S_\pm$ the two-dimensional semi-spin representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$.
Proposition 1.2 (Four-dimensional chirality).
Fix an orientation of $V$.
For an oriented orthonormal basis $v_1,\dots,v_4$ of $V$ the element $q(v_1\wedge v_2\wedge v_3\wedge v_4)=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ of $\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ depends on the orientation alone.
The operator $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$ squares to $1$ on $\Sigma$ and on $\Sigma^*$, with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$ each of multiplicity $8$.
Writing
one has, for $v\in V$ and $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$,
\rho(v)\colon S_+\otimes W\to S_-\otimes W,\qquad \rho(w)\colon S_+\otimes W\to S_+\otimes W^*,
and correspondingly on the other summands: $\rho(v)$ exchanges the four-dimensional chiralities and $\rho(w)$ preserves them.
Proof.
The element $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ is the antisymmetrisation $q$ of the oriented unit element of $\wedge^4V$, hence depends on the orientation alone.
By the Clifford relation the $v_i$ anticommute pairwise and square to $1$, hence
Moving $v_1$ through $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ meets $v_2,v_3,v_4$ once each, so $v_1\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1$; the same holds for each $v_i$, hence for every $v\in V$ by linearity.
For $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $w$ anticommutes with all four $v_i$, so $w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=(+1)(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,w$.

Since $\rho(v)$ maps $\Sigma\to\Sigma^*$, the first relation reads $\rho(v)\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma}=-\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma^*}\rho(v)$, so $\rho(v)$ maps the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $-1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$; the second relation gives $\rho(w)$ mapping the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$.
For the multiplicities, take a unit vector $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$.

The even element $v_1w$ satisfies $(v_1w)^2=-v_1^2w^2=-1$ and $v_1w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1w$, so $\rho(v_1w)$ is an invertible endomorphism of $\Sigma$ (and of $\Sigma^*$) exchanging the two eigenspaces of $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$; hence each eigenspace has dimension $16/2=8$.
Remark 1.3.
The names of the eigenspaces depend on the orientation of $V$; the opposite orientation exchanges $S_+\leftrightarrow S_-$ in all four of them.
This orientation is fixed once; Chapter 2 uses it to name the supercharges.
1.2 Fields, degrees and parities
Definition 1.4 (Fields).
The BRST fields of [ESW, Def 3.2], reduced along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56, Prop 2.20], form
F_{\rm gauge}=\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;\mathfrak g[1])\oplus\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;V_{10}^\vee\otimes\mathfrak g)\oplus\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;\Pi\Sigma\otimes\mathfrak g),
with sections $(c,A,\lambda)$.
The space of BV fields is $\mathscr E$ [C07, §4.1],
\mathscr E=F_{\rm gauge}\oplus F_{\rm gauge}^![-1]\qquad[\text{ESW, Rem 1.36}],
with antifields $(c^*,A^*,\lambda^*)$; duals are identified through $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$, the metric of $V_{10}$, the pairing $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ and $\mathrm{dvol}$.

The component of $A$ along $V$ is the connection $A|_V$, the component along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, and $\iota_wA=A(w)$ for $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ are the six scalars.
The compactly supported elements of $\mathscr E$ form $\mathscr E_c$ ($\mathcal E_c$ in [ESW, §1.1]).
The degrees are those of [ESW, Rem 1.33]: the ghost $c$ is a section in degree $-1$, which forces $A^*$ in degree $+1$ and $c^*$ in degree $+2$.
Signs follow the Koszul rule for the total parity, the sum of the $\mathbb Z$-degree and the $\mathbb Z/2$-degree modulo $2$ [ESW, §1.1].

1.3 Pairing and bracket
Definition 1.5 (Odd pairing).
The odd pairing $\langle\,,\rangle$ on $\mathscr E$ [C07, Def 4.3.1; ESW, Def 1.13, Def 1.16] is nonzero exactly between a field and its antifield.
For each of the three pairs, call the member of even total parity the even member: $A$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$; their partners $A^*$, $\lambda$, $c$ are odd.
For a section $e_0$ in the slot of an even member and a section $e_1$ in the slot of its partner,
\langle e_0,e_1\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1),\qquad \langle e_1,e_0\rangle=-\langle e_0,e_1\rangle ,

where $(e_0,e_1)$ is the fibre pairing of Definition [1.4](#b-00081); for the pair $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ it is $(e_1,e_0)$ with $(-,-)\colon\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ tensored with $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$.
Definition 1.6 (Bracket and the kernel of the identity).
The kernel $K_0$ of the identity [CG2, §7.2.3] has nonzero components exactly in the slot pairs
A\otimes A^*,\quad A^*\otimes A,\quad \lambda^*\otimes\lambda,\quad \lambda\otimes\lambda^*,\quad c^*\otimes c,\quad c\otimes c^*,

each equal to $-\delta(x-y)$ times the inverse of the fibre pairing: $(-,-)^{-1}$ tensored with the inverse metric of $V_{10}$ for $A$, $A^*$, with the canonical element of $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*$ for $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and with $1$ for $c$, $c^*$; here $x,y\in\mathbb R^4$ are the two positions and $\delta(x-y)$ is the delta distribution of the diagonal, always written with its argument.
The bracket is the odd Poisson bracket of [C07, Lemma 4.3.2], defined for $f$ local and $g$ arbitrary; it is given by the formula of [C07, §10.1] for the manifold a point,
\{f,g\}=\Delta_0(fg)-\Delta_0(f)g-(-1)^{|f|}f\Delta_0(g),\qquad \Delta_0=-\partial_{K_0},
with $\partial_\phi$ the order-two operator of [C07, §6.4] and $f$ local.
It satisfies
the graded symmetry of [ESW, Def 1.15].
Remark 1.7.
The overall sign of $\langle\,,\rangle$ is a convention: reversing it reverses $K_0$ and the bracket, and leaves the master equation $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant.
The relative signs of the three pairs are fixed by the master equation (Proposition 1.14).
1.4 The action
Definition 1.8 (Action).
The action is the dimensional reduction of [ESW, (31)]:
S=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)+(d_Ac,A^*)+([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)+\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)\Big), \tag{1.1}
with
F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A],\qquad d_A=d+[A,-],\qquad {\not d}_A=\rho\circ d_A .
Here $A$ is regarded as a one-form on $V_{10}$ constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$; $d$ acts along $\mathbb R^4$, and $d_A$, ${\not d}_A$ use all ten components of $A$.
The pairing $(F_A,F_A)$ is the Hodge pairing on $\wedge^2V_{10}^\vee$ tensored with $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$, normalised by
Every pairing in (1.1) is read with its left entry first, as printed in [ESW, (31)].
In [ESW] the full action is $S$ and the interaction is $I$; in [C07] the letter $S$ denotes the interaction.
Here $S$ is always the full action and $I$ the interaction.
Splitting $A=A|_V+A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$,

(F_A,F_A)=(F_{A|_V},F_{A|_V})+\big(d_{A|_V}A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},\,d_{A|_V}A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\big)+\big(\tfrac12[A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\wedge A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}],\,\tfrac12[A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\wedge A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}]\big),
{\not d}_A\lambda={\not d}\lambda+\rho([A|_V,\lambda])+\rho([A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},\lambda]),\qquad (d_Ac,A^*)=(dc,A^*|_V)+([A,c],A^*),
where $\rho([A,\lambda])$ is Clifford multiplication by the $V_{10}^\vee$ factor of $A$ (through the metric) together with $[-,-]$ on the $\mathfrak g$ factors, i.e. $({\not d}_A-{\not d})\lambda$.
Proposition 1.9 (Normalisation of the gauge kinetic term).
For $Q_1\in\Sigma$ put
S^{(1)}(Q_1)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)+\tfrac12(\rho(F_A)Q_1,\lambda^*)\Big)\qquad[\text{ESW, (33)}].

For abelian $\mathfrak g$ the bracket $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}$ is an affine function of the coefficient of the Hodge pairing $(F_A,F_A)$ in (1.1), and the identity $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}=0$ of [ESW, Lemma 3.4] fixes this coefficient to $-\tfrac14$.
The coefficients $+\tfrac14$ and $-\tfrac12$ (the reading of $(F_A,F_A)$ as a sum over ordered pairs of directions, twice the Hodge pairing) give a nonzero bracket.
Proof.

For abelian $\mathfrak g$ the bracket is affine in the coefficient of $(F_A,F_A)$: this coefficient times $(dA,dA)$ meets $-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair, $\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair, and $(dc,A^*)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ in $(\rho(d\,dc)Q_1,\lambda^*)=0$.

With the coefficient $-\tfrac14$ the bracket vanishes for every $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and every $\mathfrak g$: this is [ESW, Lemma 3.4] in ten dimensions, pulled back along the reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20], and for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ it holds on every element of a basis of $\Sigma$ (Remark 1.15); the part of this bracket quadratic in the fields is the abelian bracket.
With the coefficient $+\tfrac14$ the abelian bracket is a nonzero local functional at an element $Q_1\in\Sigma$ (Remark 1.15).
An affine function that vanishes at $-\tfrac14$ and is nonzero at $+\tfrac14$ has $-\tfrac14$ as its unique zero; in particular it is nonzero at $-\tfrac12$.
The free part of $S$ is
\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-\tfrac14(dA,dA)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)+(dc,A^*)\Big)\qquad[\text{C07, §1, §4.3}], \tag{1.2}
and $I=S-\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is the interaction.
Fields and kernels on $\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4$ are Fourier transformed as
\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}e^{i(p,x)}(\cdots)(p),\qquad \int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}e^{i(p,x-y)}(\cdots)(p),
with $p\in V$ and $|p|^2=(p,p)$; thus $d$ becomes $i(p,-)$.
Remark 1.10 (Real slice).
The weight is $e^{+S/\hbar}$, with $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ negative definite on the real slice [C07, §6.6].
For $A$ real with respect to the compact real form of $\mathfrak g$,
\langle A,QA\rangle=-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)\le0,

and for a fixed nonzero momentum $p$ the quadratic form on the fibre $V_{10}^\vee$ has eigenvalues, in units of $(-,-)$, equal to $-\tfrac12|p|^2$ with multiplicity $9$ and $0$ with multiplicity $1$; the zero eigenvector is the longitudinal part of $A|_V$, which lies in $\operatorname{Im}Q$.

Remark 1.12 (A sign conflict in the sources).

[ESW, Def 1.16] prints the adjointness of the BV differential as $\int\omega(e_0,Q_{BV}e_1)=(-1)^{|e_0|}\int\omega(Q_{BV}e_0,e_1)$, where $\omega$ and $Q_{BV}$ are the [ESW] names of $\langle\,,\rangle$ and $Q$.
Combined with the graded antisymmetry $\langle e_1,e_0\rangle=-\langle e_0,e_1\rangle$ of Definition 1.5 for $e_0$ even and $e_1$ odd, the printed relation gives, for $e_0=e_1=A$ in the $A$ slot,
\langle A,QA\rangle=\langle QA,A\rangle=-\langle A,QA\rangle,
hence $\langle A,QA\rangle=0$, which contradicts the kinetic term $\tfrac12\langle A,QA\rangle=-\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)$ of (1.2).
The relation of Proposition 1.11, $\langle Qe_0,e_1\rangle+(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Qe_1\rangle=0$, is the one satisfied by the action, and it is used throughout.

1.7 The classical master equation
Proposition 1.14 (Classical master equation).
For every $\mathfrak g$ as in Definition [1.1](#b-00054):
• equivalently, $\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=0$ (that is, $Q^2=0$) and $QI+\tfrac12\{I,I\}=0$.
If moreover $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]\neq0$, the master equation fixes the relative signs of the pairing and the sign of the ghost term:
• if the sign of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pairing, or of the $(c^*,c)$ pairing, or of both, is reversed relative to the $(A,A^*)$ pairing in Definition [1.5](#b-00091), then $\{S,S\}\neq0$;
• with the pairing of Definition [1.5](#b-00091) and the sign of the term $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$ reversed, $\{S,S\}\neq0$.
Proof.
Equivalence.
Write $S=\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle+I$.
Both summands are even, so by graded symmetry $\{I,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,I\}=QI$ (Proposition 1.11), and
\{S,S\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}+2\,QI+\{I,I\}.

The first term is $Q$ applied to $\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$; by the preservation of the pairing in Proposition 1.11, $\langle Qe,Qe\rangle=-(-1)^{|e|}\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$, so this term is a multiple of $\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$ and vanishes by $Q^2=0$.
This gives the equivalence of the first two items.
$\{S,S\}=0$ for every $\mathfrak g$.

The action (1.1) is the BV action of the BRST theory of [ESW, Def 3.2], built as in [ESW, Def 1.34] with the natural pairing of the shifted cotangent bundle; it satisfies $\{S,S\}=0$ for every $\mathfrak g$, and the dimensional reduction preserves it [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56].
The natural pairing differs from Definition 1.5 at most by a sign on each of the three pairs, and these signs are independent of $\mathfrak g$.
An overall sign leaves $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant.

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the density of $\{S,S\}$ computed with the pairing of Definition 1.5 vanishes as a local functional, together with $2QI+\{I,I\}$, while $QI\neq0$; for each of the three other relative sign patterns it is nonzero (Remark 1.15).
Hence the natural pairing coincides with Definition 1.5 up to an overall sign, and $\{S,S\}=0$ holds for every $\mathfrak g$.
The same exact computation gives $\{S,S\}=0$ for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$.
The relative signs.
The action is linear in the antifields, so $\{S,S\}$ has antifield number $0$ and $1$.
Each term of $\{S,S\}$ pairs a derivative along a field with a derivative along its partner and carries the sign of that pair.
The derivatives of $S$ along the antifields are the gauge transformations $A\mapsto d_Ac$, $\lambda\mapsto[c,\lambda]$, $c\mapsto\tfrac12[c,c]$.
• Antifield number $0$: the gauge variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)\big)$.
The $A$-variation enters through the $(A,A^*)$ pair and the $\lambda$-variation through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair.
• Linear in $A^*$: $[d_Ac,c]$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair against $d_A(\tfrac12[c,c])$ through the $(c^*,c)$ pair, related by the Leibniz rule $d_A[c,c]=2[d_Ac,c]$.

• Linear in $\lambda^*$: $[c,[c,\lambda]]$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair against $\tfrac12[[c,c],\lambda]$ through the $(c^*,c)$ pair, related by the Jacobi identity $2[c,[c,\lambda]]=[[c,c],\lambda]$.
• Linear in $c^*$: $[c,[c,c]]=0$.
Consider the part of $\{S,S\}$ with field content $(c,\lambda,\lambda)$, no $A$ and no antifield.
The $(c^*,c)$ pair contributes nothing to it, since $\tfrac12[c,c]$ contains two ghosts.

The $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair contributes the variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$ along $\lambda\mapsto[c,\lambda]$, and the $(A,A^*)$ pair contributes, up to the sign of that pair, a nonzero multiple of the variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,\rho([A,\lambda]))$ along $A\mapsto dc$, which is a nonzero multiple of
\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big(\lambda,\rho([dc,\lambda])\big).

With the pairing of Definition 1.5 these two contributions cancel, because $\{S,S\}=0$; reversing the sign of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair relative to the $(A,A^*)$ pair therefore turns this part of $\{S,S\}$ into twice the $(A,A^*)$ contribution.

This functional is nonzero when $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g] eq0$: choose $X,Y,Z\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,[Z,Y]) eq0$, compactly supported $\Sigma$-valued functions $s_1,s_2$ and a compactly supported function $f$ with $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(df,\Gamma(s_1,s_2)) eq0$, and put $\lambda=r_1s_1X+r_2s_2Y$, $c=r_3fZ$ with $r_1,r_2,r_3$ odd as in Definition 1.13.
Using $r_2r_3r_1=-r_1r_3r_2$, $(Y,[Z,X])=-(X,[Z,Y])$ and the symmetry of $\Gamma$,
\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big(\lambda,\rho([dc,\lambda])\big)=2\,r_1r_3r_2\,(X,[Z,Y])\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(df,\Gamma(s_1,s_2))\neq0 .
This proves the first of the last two items when the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ sign is reversed, alone or together with the $(c^*,c)$ sign.
Next consider the part with field content $(c,c,A^*)$ and no $A$.
The $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair contributes nothing to it.

The $(A,A^*)$ pair contributes the variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$ along $A\mapsto dc$, which is $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)$ up to the sign of the pair, and the $(c^*,c)$ pair contributes the variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A^*)$ along $c\mapsto\tfrac12[c,c]$, which is $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)$ up to the product of the sign of the pair and the sign of the term $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$.

They cancel with the data of Definitions 1.5 and 1.8, so reversing the $(c^*,c)$ sign alone, or the sign of $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$ alone, turns this part into twice $\pm\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)$.
On $c=r_1f_1X+r_2f_2Y$ with $[X,Y]\neq0$,
\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)=r_1r_2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big([X,Y],\,(d(f_1f_2),A^*|_V)\big),
which is nonzero for a suitable compactly supported $A^*|_V$.
Remark 1.15 (Exact verification of identities of local functionals).
Propositions 1.9 and 1.14 use the following exact computation.

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ fix bases of $\mathfrak g$, of $V_{10}$ and of $\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*$ in which the bracket, the pairings, $\rho$ and $\Gamma$ have Gaussian-rational entries.

The density of each local functional of this chapter, and of each bracket of two of them, is then a polynomial in the jets of the components of the six fields with Gaussian-rational coefficients, computed in exact arithmetic.

A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D$ without constant term vanishes on $\mathscr E_c$ when all Euler–Lagrange derivatives of $D$ vanish identically: for $e\in\mathscr E_c$, after integration by parts with compact support, $\frac{d}{ds}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D(se)$ is the integral of the Euler–Lagrange derivatives of $D$ at $se$ paired with $e$ (odd components multiplied by odd elements of an auxiliary nilpotent ring, as in Definition 1.13), so $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D(se)$ is independent of $s$ and equals its value $0$ at $s=0$.
Conversely, a nonzero Euler–Lagrange derivative shows that the functional is nonzero.
Statements that a bracket vanishes for every element of $\Sigma$ are established on every element of a basis of $\Sigma$; this suffices, because the bracket is linear in that element.
2. Superconformal symmetry as an equivariant action

The dilatation of a composite operator, and every other superconformal transformation, acts on the fields of $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory [ESW, Def 2.4, §10.3] up to gauge transformations and equations of motion.

In the BV formalism this structure is a Maurer–Cartan element of a Chevalley–Eilenberg complex, an $L_\infty$ action in the sense of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27], and it is the classical input of the equivariant observables used later.

[ESW, (32)–(34), Thm 3.3] construct it for the Poincaré supersymmetry algebra; the special conformal transformations and the special supercharges require Weyl weights, a compensating term with the six scalars, and an R-symmetry rotation in the odd bracket.

This chapter realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, the complexification of $\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)$ [SW, (7)], on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, fixes the sign conventions of the complex, writes the action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, and proves its master equation for every gauge algebra.
2.1 The algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ in complexified Euclidean form
Throughout, $x\in V$ denotes the position on $\mathbb R^4$ and $E$ the Euler vector field $E(x)=x$ of [SW, (3)]; in this chapter $E$ always means this vector field.

For a vector field $v$ on $V_{10}$, $(v,-)$ is its metric dual one-form, $L_v$ the Lie derivative [ESW, (32)], $v(-)$ the derivative along $v$, and $\operatorname{div}v$ the divergence, $L_v\,\mathrm{dvol}=(\operatorname{div}v)\,\mathrm{dvol}$.
Definition 2.1 (Even part).
The even part of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the Lie algebra of vector fields on $V_{10}=V\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ spanned by
• translations $x\mapsto v_1$, $v_1\in V$;
• rotations, the linear vector fields given by elements of $\mathfrak{so}(V)$;
• the dilatation $\Delta=2E$, the generator $\Delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1\,|\,0)$ of [SW, (17)], with $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta=-2$ on translations (Remark [2.6](#b-00254));
• special conformal fields $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$, $v_1\in V$, the special conformal field of [SW, (3)] along $v_1$;
• linear vector fields on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ given by elements of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$,
with the bracket $[v,v']=v(v')-v'(v)$.
The first four kinds are the conformal Killing vector fields of $V$; together with $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ the even part has dimension $15+15=30$.
Definition 2.2 (Odd part).
The odd part of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is $\Pi(\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*)$.
An element $Q_1\in\Sigma$ is realised by the constant spinor $Q_1$, and an element $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ by the $\Sigma$-valued function $x\mapsto\rho(x)Q_2$.
Together these span the conformal Killing spinors
x\mapsto Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\qquad Q_1\in\Sigma,\ Q_2\in\Sigma^* .
Supercharge spinors always carry a subscript, $Q_1,Q_2,\dots$, and each formula states whether they lie in $\Sigma$ or in $\Sigma^*$; the unsubscripted $Q$ is the differential of Chapter 1.
Definition 2.3 (Bracket).
On two even elements the bracket of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the bracket of vector fields, $[v,v']=v(v')-v'(v)$.
For an even element $v$ and an odd element,
[v,\,Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2]=v(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2)+\tfrac14\rho(d(v,-))(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2)-\tfrac18(\operatorname{div}v)(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2), \tag{2.1}
where $\rho$ of the two-form $d(v,-)$ means $\rho\circ q$ [ESW, (29)]; the right-hand side is again a conformal Killing spinor.
For two odd elements, with $Q_1,Q_3\in\Sigma$ and $Q_2,Q_4\in\Sigma^*$,
[Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\ Q_3+\rho(x)Q_4]=\Big(x\mapsto\Gamma\big(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\,Q_3+\rho(x)Q_4\big)\big|_V\Big)+\big(\text{rotation of }W_{\mathbb R}^\perp\big), \tag{2.2}
where $|_V$ is the orthogonal projection $V_{10}\to V$ and the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is the element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ with matrix elements
\big(w,(\text{rotation of }W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)\,w'\big)=(\rho(q(w\wedge w'))Q_1,Q_4)+(\rho(q(w\wedge w'))Q_3,Q_2),\qquad w,w'\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp .

The $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$-components of $\Gamma$ drop out of the bracket, as in the dimensional reduction of the supertranslation algebra [ESW, §2.6, Prop 2.20]; they reappear in $S^{(2)}$ (Definition 2.15).

The coefficient $1$ in front of the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is fixed by the super-Jacobi identity on triples in $\Sigma\times\Sigma\times\Sigma^*$: each term of the Jacobi sum of three odd elements contains exactly one odd–odd bracket, so the sum is affine in this coefficient; it vanishes at $1$ and is nonzero at $0$ (Remark 2.18), so $1$ is its unique zero.
Proposition 2.4 (Brackets of the named generators).
• For $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, a translation; this is [ESW, Def 2.5] after reduction.
• For $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=-\big(x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$ with $v_1=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, a special conformal field.

• For $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=\big(x\mapsto\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)|_V\big)+(\text{rotation of }W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ as in Definition [2.3](#b-00215); the dilatation part of the first summand is $\tfrac12(Q_1,Q_2)\,\Delta$, and the rest is a rotation of $V$.
• For a translation $x\mapsto v_1$: $[v_1,Q_1]=0$ for $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and $[v_1,Q_2]=\rho(v_1)Q_2\in\Sigma$ for $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$.
• For a special conformal field $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$: its bracket with $Q_1\in\Sigma$ is $\rho(v_1)Q_1\in\Sigma^*$, and with $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ it is $0$.
• $[\Delta,Q_1]=-Q_1$ for $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and $[\Delta,Q_2]=+Q_2$ for $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$.
Proof.
The first two items follow from [(2.2)](#b-00219): for $Q_2=Q_4=0$ the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ vanishes; for $Q_1=Q_3=0$ it vanishes as well, and for $v\in V$
(v,\Gamma(\rho(x)Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2))=(\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)Q_1,Q_2)=2(v,x)(x,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2))-(x,x)(v,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)),
using $\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)=2(v,x)\rho(x)-(x,x)\rho(v)$ from the Clifford relation and $(\rho(x)Q_1,Q_2)=(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)$.
Projecting to $V$ gives $-\big((x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$.

For $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ and $v\in V$, $(v,\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2))=(\rho(x)\rho(v)Q_1,Q_2)$; the part symmetric under $x\leftrightarrow v$ is $\tfrac12(\rho(x)\rho(v)+\rho(v)\rho(x))=(x,v)$, so the linear vector field $x\mapsto\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)|_V$ equals $(Q_1,Q_2)\,E=\tfrac12(Q_1,Q_2)\,\Delta$ plus an antisymmetric linear field, i.e. a rotation.
For the even–odd brackets use (2.1).
For $v=2E$: $(v,-)=d(x,x)$ is closed, $\operatorname{div}(2E)=8$, $2E(Q_1)=0$ and $2E(\rho(x)Q_2)=2\rho(x)Q_2$, so $[\Delta,Q_1]=-Q_1$ and $[\Delta,\rho(x)Q_2]=(2-1)\rho(x)Q_2$.
For a translation, $(v,-)$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}v=0$, so (2.1) reduces to $v_1(\rho(x)Q_2)=\rho(v_1)Q_2$.
For $v=(x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x)$,
so $\tfrac14\rho(d(v,-))-\tfrac18\operatorname{div}v=\rho(x)\rho(v_1)-(x,v_1)+(v_1,x)=\rho(x)\rho(v_1)$.
On a constant $Q_1\in\Sigma$ this gives $x\mapsto\rho(x)\rho(v_1)Q_1$, the realisation of $\rho(v_1)Q_1\in\Sigma^*$.

Proposition 2.5 (Identification with $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$).
The bracket of Definition [2.3](#b-00215) has the following properties.
• The dimension is $30|32$, and the bracket of two elements of the ten named subspaces lies in their span.
• The bracket is graded antisymmetric and satisfies the super-Jacobi identity.

• The $V$-part of every odd–odd bracket is a conformal Killing vector field of $V$; the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is nonzero for $\Sigma\times\Sigma^*$ and vanishes for $\Sigma\times\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*$.

• The block rule of the supermatrix presentation [SW, (17), (19)] holds for every pair of the ten named subspaces: their bracket lies in the block with the row of the first subspace and the column of the second when the column of the first equals the row of the second, plus the block with the row of the second and the column of the first when the column of the second equals the row of the first, and vanishes otherwise.
• $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta$ is diagonal on the named subspaces with the eigenvalues of the table above, which are those of $\Delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1\,|\,0)$ in [SW, (17)].
• The Killing form $\mathrm{str}(\mathrm{ad}_{x_1}\mathrm{ad}_{x_2})$ for $x_1,x_2\in\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, with $\mathrm{str}$ the supertrace [SW, after (17)], vanishes identically.

• The algebra equals its derived algebra and has trivial centre; its even part is the sum of the two commuting ideals formed by the conformal Killing vector fields of $V$ and by $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, each of dimension $15$ with nondegenerate Killing form.
These are the properties by which the algebra is identified with the complexification $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ of $\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)$ [SW, (7), (17)].
Proof.
The dimension count is $4+6+1+4+15=30$ and $16+16=32$.

Every other item is a bilinear or trilinear identity in the arguments, or a statement about the structure constants; each is established on all ordered pairs and all ordered triples of elements of a basis adapted to the ten named subspaces (Remark 2.18), hence for all arguments.
Remark 2.6 (Dilatation normalisation).

The dilatation is the $\Delta$ of [SW, (17)], the vector field $2E$, with $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta$ eigenvalue $-2$ on translations, $+2$ on special conformal fields, $-1$ on $\Sigma$, $+1$ on $\Sigma^*$ and $0$ on rotations.
The generator called $\Delta$ in [SW, (3)] is the vector field $-E$, and the bosonic part of the $\Delta$ of [SW, (12)] is $E$.
Every cochain component is linear in its arguments, so a component evaluated on $2E$ is $-2$ times the same component evaluated on $-E$:
and a coefficient computed in the normalisation of [SW, (3)] is converted to the normalisation used here by the factor $-2$.

Definition 2.12 (Arity one).
For a conformal Killing vector field $v$ of $V$, or $v$ the linear vector field of an element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, regarded as a vector field on $V_{10}$:

Here $A$ is a one-form on $V_{10}$ constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56] and $L_v$ is its Lie derivative on $V_{10}$: for $v$ on $V$, $L_v(A|_V)$ is the Lie derivative of the one-form and $L_v(\iota_wA)=v(\iota_wA)$; for $v$ the linear vector field of an element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, $\iota_w(L_vA)=\iota_{v(w)}A$.

For $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$, with conformal Killing spinor $x\mapsto\rho(x)Q_2$:

where $\rho(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ is Clifford multiplication by the $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$-component of $A$, with its $\mathfrak g$ factor kept.

The divergences are $\operatorname{div}v=0$ for translations, rotations and $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, $\operatorname{div}(2E)=8$, and $\operatorname{div}v=-8(v_1,x)$ for $v=(x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x)$.

Example 2.13 (The dilatation).
For $\Delta=2E$: $(2E,-)=d(x,x)$ is closed, so $\rho(d(v,-))=0$, and $\operatorname{div}(2E)=8$.
On the one-form $A|_V$, $L_{2E}A|_V=2E(A|_V)+2A|_V$ with $E(-)$ acting componentwise, and on the scalars $L_{2E}\iota_wA+\tfrac14\cdot8\,\iota_wA=2E(\iota_wA)+2\iota_wA$.
Hence

in the normalisation of Remark [2.6](#b-00254), $A$, $\lambda$, $c$ carry the weights $2$, $3$, $0$, i.e. the Weyl weights $1$, $\tfrac32$, $0$ with respect to $E$.
Proposition 2.14 (The coefficients are forced).

Replace the coefficients $\tfrac14$ (spin), $\tfrac38$ (Weyl weight of $\lambda$) and $\tfrac14$ (Weyl weight of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$) in (2.5), and the coefficient $-1$ of the last term of (2.7), by unknowns.
For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the arity-one equation $\{S,S^{(1)}(x_1)\}=0$ at one element $x_1$ of each type determines the unknowns uniquely:
• a rotation in $\mathfrak{so}(V)$, and an element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$: spin coefficient $\tfrac14$;
• $\Delta$: $(\tfrac38,\tfrac14)$ for the two Weyl weights;
• a special conformal field: $(\tfrac14,\tfrac38,\tfrac14)$;
With these values the arity-one equation holds for every element of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ and every $\mathfrak g$ (Theorem 2.20).
The Weyl weight $1$ of $A|_V$ is carried by $L_v$ and the weight $0$ of $c$ by $v.c$.

For each type the bracket $\{S,S^{(1)}(x_1)\}$ is affine in the unknowns.

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and one element $x_1$ of each type, its density is a polynomial in the jets of the fields with coefficients affine in the unknowns, and the conditions that all Euler–Lagrange derivatives vanish form a linear system whose unique solution is the one stated (Remark 2.18).

2.4 Quadratic-antifield terms and the end of the tower
Definition 2.15 (Arity two).

For $Q_1,Q_2$ each in $\Sigma$ or in $\Sigma^*$, $S^{(2)}(Q_1,Q_2)$ is [ESW, (34)] evaluated pointwise on the conformal Killing spinors, i.e. every $Q_i\in\Sigma^*$ is replaced by the $\Sigma$-valued function $x\mapsto\rho(x)Q_i$ in
S^{(2)}(Q_1,Q_2)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(\tfrac14\big(\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2),\Gamma(\lambda^*,\lambda^*)\big)-\tfrac12(Q_1,\lambda^*)(Q_2,\lambda^*)-\big(\iota_{\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)}A,\,c^*\big)\Big), \tag{2.8}

with $\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)\in V_{10}$ the full ten-component $\Gamma$-pairing, so that the gauge parameter is $\iota_{\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)}A=\iota_{\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V}A|_V+\iota_{\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}}A$.
The field-dependent gauge parameter $\iota_{\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)}A$ of the $c^*$ term is:
• $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma$: $\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)$ constant, as in [ESW, (34)];
• $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)$, linear in $x$;

• $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $\Gamma(\rho(x)Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)$, with $V$-part $-\big((x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$, $v_1=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$-part $-(x,x)\,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ (proof of Proposition [2.4](#b-00223)).

Proposition 2.16 (The tower stops at arity two).
For every $\mathfrak g$ and all arguments, with $S^{(k\ge3)}=0$:
• the components of [(2.4)](#b-00285) of arity $\ge4$ hold;
• the arity-three components with at most one odd argument hold;
• the arity-three components with three odd arguments hold.
Proof.
$S^{(2)}$ contains the fields $A$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$ and none of their partners $A^*$, $\lambda$, $c$, and the bracket pairs each field with its partner (Definition 1.6); hence the first item.

In arity $4$, with $S^{(3)}=S^{(4)}=0$, Lemma 2.11 leaves the three brackets $\{S^{(2)},S^{(2)}\}$, which vanish; when an argument is even, every surviving term contains $S^{(2)}$ with an even argument and vanishes.
In arity $n\ge5$ every term contains $S^{(k)}$ with $k\ge3$ or $\{S^{(k)},S^{(l)}\}$ with $k+l=n$, hence $k\ge3$ or $l\ge3$, and vanishes.

In arity $3$ with at most one odd argument, every term contains $S^{(2)}$ with an even entry, because among $[x_i,x_j]$ and $x_k$, and among any two of the arguments, at most one entry is odd; so every term vanishes.
In arity $3$ with three odd arguments, every $[x_i,x_j]$ is even, so the equation of Lemma 2.11 reduces to the cyclic sum $\sum_{\rm cyc}\{S^{(1)}(x_1),S^{(2)}(x_2,x_3)\}$.

In this bracket, $S^{(2)}$ supplies $A$ and $\lambda^*$, whose partners $A^*$ and $\lambda$ occur in $S^{(1)}(x_1)$ exclusively through the term $-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)$, with $Q_1$ replaced by the conformal Killing spinor of $x_1$; the last term of (2.7) contains $A$ and $\lambda^*$ and has vanishing bracket with $S^{(2)}$.

No derivative acts on the spinors, so the cyclic sum is computed pointwise in $x$ exactly as in the proof of [ESW, Lemma 3.7], with $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ replaced by the values of the three conformal Killing spinors at $x$; it vanishes by [ESW, Assumption 3.1], which holds for the ten-dimensional $\Sigma=S_+$ by [ESW, Thm 2.10] (list after [ESW, Assumption 3.1]), and the Clifford relation.

Remark 2.18 (Exact verification on a basis).
The computer-assisted statements of this chapter are exact identities established on a basis.

Fix a basis of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ adapted to the ten named subspaces, with $4+3+3+1+4+15$ even and $8+8+8+8$ odd elements, in which $\rho$, $\Gamma$ and the pairing $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ have Gaussian-rational entries.

The bracket of Definition 2.3 is computed in exact arithmetic on every ordered pair of basis elements; its values are expanded in the basis, and graded antisymmetry, the super-Jacobi identity on every ordered triple, the Killing form and the block rule on every ordered pair, the eigenvalues of $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta$, the derived algebra, the centre and the Killing forms of the two even ideals are computed from these structure constants.
With the coefficient $0$ in place of $1$ in front of the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ in (2.2), the super-Jacobi identity fails.

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$, with the data of Remark 1.15, every component of (2.4) of arity $1$, $2$ and $3$ is evaluated on every unordered tuple of basis elements, repetitions allowed, with at least two odd elements in arity $3$; each is a local functional whose density is a polynomial in the jets of the fields with Gaussian-rational coefficients, and it vanishes when all its Euler–Lagrange derivatives vanish identically (Remark 1.15).

All these identities are multilinear in their arguments, and the components of (2.4) are graded antisymmetric under exchange of arguments (Definition 2.7); the identities on basis tuples therefore hold for all arguments.
Lemma 2.19 (Colour reduction).

Consider local functionals that are finite sums of terms, each the product of a polynomial in the jets of the $V_{10}$-, spinor- and form-components of the fields, independent of $\mathfrak g$, and a tree tensor in the $\mathfrak g$-components of at most five fields: a multilinear form on $\mathfrak g^k$, $k\le5$, obtained from copies of $([-,-],-)$ by contraction with the inverse pairing $(-,-)^{-1}$ along a tree, or the pairing $(-,-)$ itself for $k=2$.

If the Euler–Lagrange derivatives of the density of such a functional vanish identically for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, they vanish identically for every Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing.
Proof.
By invariance of the pairing, every tree tensor with $k$ legs is a sign times $(b(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}),X_k)$ for a bracket monomial $b$ of $X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}\in\mathfrak g$, each used once.

Hence the tree tensors with $k$ legs are the values of a linear map, natural in $\mathfrak g$ and equivariant under permutations of the legs, from the space of formal trees modulo antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity, which is the multilinear part of the free Lie algebra on $k-1$ letters, of dimension $(k-2)!$.

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ this map has rank $1$, $1$, $2$, $6$ for $k=2,3,4,5$, computed exactly, so it is injective for $k\le5$, and averaging a left inverse over the permutations of the legs gives an equivariant left inverse.
A functional of the stated form is therefore the evaluation in $\mathfrak g$ of a formal expression, a sum of jet polynomials times formal trees.

Its Euler–Lagrange derivative along a field, paired with a fixed element of $\mathfrak g$ treated as one more leg, is again of this form, because differentiation acts on the jet polynomials and leaves the tree.

The equivariant left inverse acts on the trees alone; applied to the vanishing $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ evaluation it shows that the formal Euler–Lagrange derivatives vanish, hence their evaluations vanish for every $\mathfrak g$.
Theorem 2.20 (Master equation of the equivariant action).

For every Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing, $S_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}=S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, with $S^{(1)}$, $S^{(2)}$ of Definitions [2.12](#b-00307)–[2.15](#b-00332) and $S^{(k\ge3)}=0$, is an action of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on $(\mathscr E,\langle\,,\rangle,S)$: it satisfies [(2.4)](#b-00285), and $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}=I+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ satisfies $(d_{CE}+Q)I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}+\tfrac12\{I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)},I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}\}=0$.
Proof.
By Lemma 2.11 it suffices to prove the components.
Arity $0$ is Proposition 1.14.
The components of arity $\ge4$, and of arity $3$ with at most one or with three odd arguments, hold for every $\mathfrak g$ by Proposition 2.16.

The remaining components, of arities $1$ and $2$ and of arity $3$ with exactly two odd arguments, vanish for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ for all arguments (Remark 2.18).

Each of them is of the form of Lemma 2.19: every term of $S$, $S^{(1)}$, $S^{(2)}$ is a tree tensor in at most four, three and two $\mathfrak g$-components respectively, built from $(-,-)$ and $[-,-]$; the bracket of Definition 1.6 contracts one leg of each factor with the inverse pairing and joins two trees into a tree; so every term has at most $4+3-2=5$ legs.
By Lemma 2.19 these components vanish for every $\mathfrak g$.
The equation for $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}$ is [ESW, Rem 1.29].
On the subalgebra of Axiom 2.17 the statement is [ESW, Thm 3.3].

3. Costello's data with a UV boundary

Costello's renormalisation needs a gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$, the heat kernel of $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ and the propagator $P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt$ [C07, §6.5], and its axioms [C07, Def 4.3.3] are formulated on a compact manifold; [C07, §5.2] records that Yang–Mills theory in second-order form lies outside them.
On Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ we keep a single regulator, the lower Schwinger limit $\varepsilon$, and set the upper limit to $\infty$, so that $\varepsilon$ is the single scale of the construction.

This chapter constructs a Feynman-gauge operator $Q^{GF}$ that satisfies three of the five axioms, identifies the two that fail, and proves the identities that hold with these data: $QP(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon$, the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity of $Q$ at scale $\infty$ on sections with vanishing moments together with the zero-mode classes that $Q$ has on compactly supported sections, and the one-loop formula for the graph expansion.

Proposition 3.2 (The Laplacian).

• $H:=[Q,Q^{GF}]=QQ^{GF}+Q^{GF}Q=d^*d+dd^*$, the Hodge Laplacian of flat $\mathbb R^4$, which acts on every component function of every slot as the positive Laplacian of functions; in momentum space $H=|p|^2$.

• Among operators with the arrows of Definition [3.1](#b-00371) and arbitrary coefficients in place of the four coefficients $-2$, $-1$, $1$, $-1$ of the table, these are the unique ones for which $H$ is the componentwise Laplacian.
Proof.
Using Proposition [1.11](#b-00135), slot by slot:

\begin{aligned}

A:&\quad QQ^{GF}A=Q\big(-d^*(A|_V)\big)=dd^*(A|_V),\qquad Q^{GF}QA=Q^{GF}\big(-\tfrac12d^*dA\big)=d^*dA;\\
A^*:&\quad QQ^{GF}A^*=Q(-2A^*)=d^*dA^*,\qquad Q^{GF}QA^*=Q^{GF}\big(d^*(A^*|_V)\big)=dd^*(A^*|_V);\\
c^*:&\quad QQ^{GF}c^*=Q(dc^*)=d^*dc^*,\qquad Q^{GF}Qc^*=0;\\
\lambda:&\quad Q^{GF}Q\lambda=-{\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}{\not d}\lambda=d^*d\lambda,\qquad QQ^{GF}\lambda=0;\\
\lambda^*:&\quad QQ^{GF}\lambda^*=-{\not d}\,{\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}\lambda^*=d^*d\lambda^*,\qquad Q^{GF}Q\lambda^*=0,
\end{aligned}

where on a plane wave $e^{i(p,x)}$ the Dirac operators become $i ho(p)$, so that $-{ ot d}|_{\Sigma^*}{ ot d}$ and $-{ ot d}\,{ ot d}|_{\Sigma^*}$ become $ ho(p) ho(p)=(p,p)=|p|^2$ by the Clifford relation, the symbol of $d^*d$.

On $A|_V$ and on $A^*|_V$ the sum $d^*d+dd^*$ is the Hodge Laplacian on one-forms of flat $\mathbb R^4$, which is the Laplacian $d^*d$ of functions on each component; on $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ and $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ the term $dd^*$ is absent and $d^*d$ is the Laplacian of each scalar.
Since $H$ is a constant-coefficient scalar operator, it commutes with $Q$ and $Q^{GF}$.

For the uniqueness, each coefficient is fixed by one slot: the $c$ slot fixes the coefficient of $A\mapsto-d^*(A|_V)$, the transverse part of $A$ fixes the coefficient of $A^*\mapsto-2A^*$ (because $Q$ contributes $-\tfrac12$), the $c^*$ slot fixes the coefficient of $c^*\mapsto dc^*$, and the $\lambda$ slot fixes the coefficient of $\lambda^*\mapsto-{\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}\lambda^*$.
Proposition 3.3 (Adjointness).
For all $e_0,e_1\in\mathscr E_c$,
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle,\qquad \langle Qe_0,e_1\rangle=-(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Qe_1\rangle ;
equivalently $(Q^{GF}\otimes1-1\otimes Q^{GF})K_0=0$ and $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_0=0$.
Thus $Q^{GF}$ has the adjointness opposite to that of $Q$.
Proof.
The statement for $Q$ is Proposition 1.11.
For $Q^{GF}$ the pairing vanishes outside the following cases.
For $e_0,e_1$ in the $A^*$ slot (odd),
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1),\qquad \langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle=-\langle-2e_1,e_0\rangle=2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1).
For $e_0$ in the $A$ slot and $e_1$ in the $c^*$ slot (both even),
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=-\langle e_1,-d^*(e_0|_V)\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(de_1,e_0),\qquad \langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,de_1).
For $e_0,e_1$ in the $\lambda^*$ slot (even), with the symmetry of $\rho(v)$ and integration by parts,
The case $e_0$ in the $c^*$ slot, $e_1$ in the $A$ slot follows by graded antisymmetry.
In each case $\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle$.
Remark 3.4 (Names of the adjointness relations in the sources).

[C07, §4.3] calls $Q$ “self adjoint” and [C07, Def 4.3.3(1)] calls $Q^{GF}$ “skew self adjoint”; [C07, §1, §1.1, §2.1] and [CG2, §7.2.1] use the opposite names, $Q$ skew self adjoint and $Q^{GF}$ self adjoint.
The relations of Proposition 3.3 fix the content, and condition (1) of [C07, Def 4.3.3] is read here as: $Q^{GF}$ has the adjointness opposite to that of $Q$.
The printed adjointness relation of [ESW, Def 1.16] is discussed in Remark 1.12.
Proposition 3.5 (Axioms of a gauge-fixing operator).
Of the conditions of [C07, Def 4.3.3], three hold:
• (1), read as in Remark [3.4](#b-00395): Proposition [3.3](#b-00383);
• (2): every component of $Q^{GF}$ has order $0$ or $1$;
• (4): $H=d^*d+dd^*$, the componentwise Laplacian, is a generalised Laplacian (Proposition [3.2](#b-00375)).
Condition (3) fails: $(Q^{GF})^2$ vanishes on the slots of $c$, $A$, $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and
(Q^{GF})^2A^*=2\,d^*(A^*|_V)\ \ (\text{in the slot of }c),\qquad (Q^{GF})^2c^*=-2\,dc^*\ \ (\text{in the slot of }A|_V).
Condition (5) fails: $\operatorname{Im}Q\cap\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}\neq0$, since for every nonzero $c\in\mathscr E_c$ in the ghost slot
Qc=-dc=Q^{GF}\big(\tfrac12dc\ \text{in the slot of }A^*|_V\big).
Moreover $\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}$ pairs nontrivially with itself: for $e_0$ in the $A^*$ slot and $e_1$ in the $c^*$ slot,
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,de_1).
Proof.

$(Q^{GF})^2A^*=Q^{GF}(-2A^*)=-2\big(-d^*(A^*|_V)\big)$ and $(Q^{GF})^2c^*=Q^{GF}(dc^*)=-2\,dc^*$; on the other slots the image of $Q^{GF}$ lies in the slots of $c$ and $\lambda$, where $Q^{GF}$ vanishes.
For (5), $Q^{GF}(\tfrac12dc)=-2\cdot\tfrac12dc$.
The last formula is $\langle-2e_0,de_1\rangle$ with $-2e_0$ in the $A$ slot.
Remark 3.6 (Consequences of the two failures).

Three statements of [C07] use (3) or (5): [C07, Lemma 6.5.1] ($P(0,\infty)$ inverts $Q\colon\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}\to\operatorname{Im}Q$; its proof uses $(Q^{GF})^2=0$), the real-slice Gaussian over $(\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF})_{\mathbb R}$ of [C07, §6.6], and [C07, Lemma 6.6.2].
Indeed $\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}$ contains the whole $A$ slot, on which $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ has the longitudinal zero eigenvector (Remark 1.10).
The arguments below use $Q^2=0$, $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$, $[Q,H]=0$ and the adjointness relations; Theorem 3.19 takes the place of [C07, Lemma 6.5.1].
Remark 3.7 (Feynman gauge).
In momentum space the $A\otimes A$ component of the propagator $P(0,\infty)$ (Proposition 3.11 at $\varepsilon=0$) is $2(-,-)^{-1}\otimes(\text{inverse metric of }V_{10})\,|p|^{-2}$.

It is the inverse of the second variation of $-\big(\tfrac12\langle A,QA\rangle-\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)\big)=\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,HA)$, i.e. the covariance of the weight $e^{+S/\hbar}$ for the Yang–Mills kinetic term completed by the Feynman-gauge term $-\tfrac14(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$; it has the eigenvalue $2(-,-)^{-1}|p|^{-2}$, positive, in all ten directions of $V_{10}$.
Restricted to $\lambda$, the propagator $P(0,\infty)$ is minus the inverse of the second variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$.

Definition 3.8 (Heat kernel).

For $t>0$, $K_t\in\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ is the kernel with the components of $K_0$ (Definition 1.6) with $\delta(x-y)$ replaced by $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$; in momentum space this factor is $e^{-t|p|^2}$.
The kernel
L_t=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t
represents $Q^{GF}e^{-tH}$ [C07, §6.5].
On $\mathbb R^4$,
K_\infty:=\lim_{t\to\infty}K_t=0,
pointwise in $x-y$, and in momentum space for every $p\neq0$.

(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_t=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}K_t+(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t=0\qquad[\text{C07, §6.5}].

$K_t=(e^{-tH}\otimes1)K_0$, $[Q,H]=0$ and $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_0=0$ give the first identity.
