Remark 3.13 (Two objects at $t=\varepsilon$).
The lower end of the Schwinger integral carries two different kernels.

By (3.2), $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$ governs the $\varepsilon$-dependence of every graph: for a graph $\gamma$ whose value is the integral of $f_\gamma$ over the Schwinger times $t_e\in[\varepsilon,\infty)$ of its edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5], $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the value is minus the sum over $e\in E(\gamma)$ of $\varepsilon f_\gamma$ with $t_e=\varepsilon$, that is, with the edge $e$ carrying $L_\varepsilon$.
The singular coefficients ($\varepsilon^{-1}$, $\log\varepsilon$) and the scaling behaviour therefore sit on $L_\varepsilon$ edges.

By (3.1), $K_\varepsilon$ governs the action of $Q$ (Theorem 3.17): the obstruction to the quantum master equation and the $Q$-variation of observables sit on edges carrying $K_\varepsilon$, or $K_\varepsilon-K_0$, and on the counterterm vertices $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$ (Definition 3.15; the counterterm $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is constructed in Chapter 4), together with their $\delta$-derivatives for observables (Chapter 5).
3.3 The UV-boundary identity
Remark 3.14 (Functionals on $\mathbb R^4$).

On $\mathbb R^4$ the operators $\partial_{K_t}$ and $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ [C07, §6.4] and the brackets below act on functionals of compactly supported sections, $\mathscr O(\mathscr E_c)\supset\mathscr O_l(\mathscr E)$ [C07, Def 4.2.2].

The interaction, its counterterms and their flows are taken modulo constants [CG2, §7.2.6]; the observables of Chapter 5 keep their constant terms, which depend on the four-form $\omega$ and carry the subtraction of the expectation value.

A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$, such as $S$, $I$ or a counterterm, is a density modulo total derivatives, and on it these operators are evaluated graph by graph (Proposition 3.22), with compactly supported legs.
For the interaction and its counterterms constants are discarded because a contraction that uses every field of a translation-invariant functional is proportional to the volume of $\mathbb R^4$.

If the Taylor component of a functional, evaluated on compactly supported sections in its remaining arguments, is an integrable kernel in the two contracted positions, its contraction with $K_t$ is bounded by $(4\pi t)^{-2}$ times the integral of the absolute value of that kernel and tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$.

This applies to every local functional $\int\omega\,(\text{density})$ with $\omega$ a compactly supported four-form [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3], to every local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$ at least quadratic in the fields, and to the bracket of two such functionals: a contraction of two legs at one point is a density times $(4\pi t)^{-2}$, and a contraction between two such functionals pairs two compactly supported densities through $K_t$.

For a linear functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c^*,X)$, $X\in\mathfrak g$, the contraction integrates $K_t$ over one position, and the integral of the scalar factor $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$ over $x$ equals $1$ for every $t$; these linear functionals are the zero-mode classes of Theorem 3.19.
Definition 3.15 (Scale-$\varepsilon$ Laplacian and bracket).

\Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}\quad[\text{C07, §10.1}],\qquad \{f,g\}_\varepsilon=\Delta_\varepsilon(fg)-\Delta_\varepsilon(f)g-(-1)^{|f|}f\Delta_\varepsilon(g)\quad[\text{CG2, §7.2.8}],
the second with the Laplacian $\Delta_\varepsilon$ of [C07] in the product rule of [CG2].

At scale $\infty$ the kernel is $K_\infty:=0$ (Definition 3.8); accordingly $\Delta_\infty:=-\partial_{K_\infty}=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$ identically, on every functional, and this is the scale-$\infty$ structure used throughout.

On functionals whose contracted Taylor components are integrable kernels (Remark 3.14), in particular on local functionals with a compactly supported four-form, on local functionals $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$ at least quadratic in the fields, and on brackets of two such, it is also the limit $t\to\infty$ of $\Delta_t$ and $\{-,-\}_t$.
Definition 3.16 (Renormalisation group flow).
For an even $\phi\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$ and an even functional $J$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$,
W(\phi,J)=\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\qquad[\text{CG2, §7.2.7}],
which is $\Gamma(\phi,J)$ of [C07, Def 6.6.1].
The letter $W$ with two arguments always denotes this flow; $W$ alone is the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10], and $\Gamma$ is reserved for the $\Gamma$-pairing of [ESW, (28)].
Theorem 3.17 (UV-boundary identity).
On functionals with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))$ (Chapter 2), as formal power series in $\hbar$,
(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\,(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon). \tag{3.3}
Here $Q^{GF}$ is the operator of Definition [3.1](#b-00371).
Proof.
By [C07, §6.4], $[\partial_\phi,Q]=\partial_{Q\phi}$ for $\phi\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$, with $Q$ acting on $\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ as $Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q$.

\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}Q-Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{K_\varepsilon}=-\Delta_\varepsilon ,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}Q+\Delta_\varepsilon .
The operators $\partial_\phi$ mutually commute [C07, §6.4], so $\Delta_\varepsilon$ commutes with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$, and by induction on $n$
Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^n=\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^nQ+n\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^{n-1}\Delta_\varepsilon .
Multiplying by $\hbar^n/n!$ and summing over $n$,
Q\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}Q+\hbar\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\Delta_\varepsilon .

Finally $d_{CE}$ acts on the arguments in $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ and $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ on the fields; $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ is a kernel on the fields, independent of the arguments of the cochains, so $[\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)},d_{CE}]=0$.
Each step uses $Q^2=0$, (3.1) and the algebra of the operators $\partial_\phi$.
Corollary 3.18 (Master equations at the two ends).

Let $J$ be an even functional with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))[[\hbar]]$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$ when the arguments of the cochains are counted as fields, as in [CG2, §13.2.2], and let $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}\big)$ be its flow (Definition 3.16).
Then
(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon)e^{J/\hbar}=0\iff(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}=0,
and the two sides are equivalent to
(d_{CE}+Q)J+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J=0,\qquad (d_{CE}+Q)\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=0 .
Proof.
Apply (3.3) to $e^{J/\hbar}$; the operator $e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}$ is invertible.
This is [C07, Lemma 10.2.2] with the second scale at $\infty$, where $\Delta_\infty=0$.

For an even $J$, the product rule of Definition 3.15, applied to the powers $J^n$, gives $\Delta_\varepsilon e^{J/\hbar}=e^{J/\hbar}\big(\hbar^{-1}\Delta_\varepsilon J+\tfrac12\hbar^{-2}\{J,J\}_\varepsilon\big)$, while $d_{CE}+Q$ is a derivation, $(d_{CE}+Q)e^{J/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}e^{J/\hbar}(d_{CE}+Q)J$; this is the equivalence of [C07, §10.1] with $\Delta_\varepsilon$ in place of $\Delta_0$.
3.4 Acyclicity at scale infinity
For a kernel $\phi\in\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ write $\phi\star$ for the operator it represents [C07, §6.3].
Thus $K_t\star=e^{-tH}$, and $P(\varepsilon,\infty)\star=\int_\varepsilon^\infty Q^{GF}e^{-tH}dt$; $P(0,\infty)\star$ is the limit $\varepsilon\to0$.

A Schwartz section of the BV bundle is a section whose components are Schwartz functions on $\mathbb R^4$; its moments are the integrals $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,f\,e$ with $f$ a polynomial function on $\mathbb R^4$.
A Schwartz section is moment-free when all its moments vanish, equivalently when its Fourier transform (Chapter 1) vanishes to infinite order at $p=0$.
The moment-free Schwartz sections form a closed subspace of the Schwartz sections, with the induced topology.
Theorem 3.19 (Acyclicity at scale $\infty$).

For every $\alpha\in\mathscr E_c$ the integral $P(0,\infty)\star\alpha=\int_0^\infty Q^{GF}e^{-tH}\alpha\,dt$ converges to a smooth section, bounded together with its first derivatives by a multiple of $(1+|x|)^{-2}$, and
Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha\big)+P(0,\infty)\star(Q\alpha)=\alpha ; \tag{3.4}
in kernel form, $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(0,\infty)=K_0$.
Moreover:
• The moment-free Schwartz sections form a space stable under $Q$, $Q^{GF}$, $e^{-tH}$ and $P(0,\infty)\star$, on which $P(0,\infty)\star$ acts continuously and (3.4) holds.
Thus $P(0,\infty)\star$ is a contracting homotopy for $Q$ there: every moment-free Schwartz section $e$ with $Qe=0$ equals $Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star e\big)$, with $P(0,\infty)\star e$ moment-free.
• Zero-mode classes.

Let $e_0$ be a section in the slot of $c$, of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ or of $\lambda$ whose components are polynomial functions on $\mathbb R^4$, with $Qe_0=0$: a constant ghost $e_0=X\in\mathfrak g$, a section of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ with harmonic polynomial components, or a polynomial solution of ${\not d}e_0=0$.
The linear functional $e\mapsto\langle e_0,e\rangle$ on $\mathscr E_c$ is $Q$-closed and is $Q$-exact for no $e_0\neq0$, and it vanishes on moment-free Schwartz sections.
For a constant ghost $X$ it is $-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c^*,X)$.
For each bound on the polynomial degree of $e_0$ these functionals span a finite-dimensional space.
Proof.
Compactly supported sections.

Each component of $e^{-tH}\alpha$ is the convolution of a component of $\alpha$ with $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x|^2/4t}$, so $e^{-tH}\alpha$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $(4\pi t)^{-2}$ times $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|\alpha|$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|d\alpha|$, and by the suprema of $|\alpha|$ and $|d\alpha|$ for $t\le1$.

Since $Q^{GF}$ has constant coefficients and order at most $1$, $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^4}|Q^{GF}e^{-tH}\alpha|$ is integrable on $(0,\infty)$; the same bounds for the derivatives allow $Q$ to pass under the integral.

At a point $x$ with $\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)\ge1$, $|e^{-tH}\alpha(x)|\le(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)^2/4t}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|\alpha|$, and
\int_0^\infty(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)^2/4t}\,dt=\frac{1}{4\pi^2\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)^2},
which gives the bound by a multiple of $(1+|x|)^{-2}$; the first derivatives obey the same bound.
Since $[Q,H]=0$, $Q^{GF}e^{-tH}Q\alpha=Q^{GF}Qe^{-tH}\alpha$, and
The limit vanishes because $|e^{-tH}\alpha|\le(4\pi t)^{-2}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|\alpha|$; this is $K_\infty=0$.
The kernel form is (3.1) at $\varepsilon\to0$ with $K_\varepsilon\to K_0$.
Moment-free sections.

In momentum space $Q$ and $Q^{GF}$ act by multiplication with the matrices of polynomials in $p$ of Proposition 1.11 and Definition 3.1, $e^{-tH}$ by $e^{-t|p|^2}$, and $P(0,\infty)\star$ by the matrix of $Q^{GF}$ times $\int_0^\infty e^{-t|p|^2}dt=|p|^{-2}$.
The first three preserve Schwartz functions of $p$ that vanish to infinite order at $p=0$.

For such a function $h$ and every $n$, Taylor's formula at $p=0$ bounds every derivative $\partial^\beta h$ on $|p|\le1$ by $|p|^n$ times a multiple of the supremum of the derivatives of $h$ of order $n+|\beta|$ on the unit ball, while every derivative of order $k$ of $|p|^{-2}$ is bounded by a multiple of $|p|^{-2-k}$; by the Leibniz rule every derivative of order $k$ of $|p|^{-2}h$ is bounded on $0<|p|\le1$ by $|p|^{n-2-k}$ times continuous seminorms of $h$.
Hence $|p|^{-2}h$ extends smoothly by $0$ at $p=0$ and vanishes there to infinite order; on $|p|\ge1$ the derivatives of $|p|^{-2}$ are bounded, so rapid decay and the seminorm bounds persist.
This proves stability and continuity.
For $p\neq0$ the matrices satisfy
by Proposition [3.2](#b-00375), and both sides of [(3.4)](#b-00487) vanish to infinite order at $p=0$; this gives [(3.4)](#b-00487) on moment-free Schwartz sections.
Zero-mode classes.

The table of Proposition 1.11 gives $Qe_0=-de_0$ on the ghost slot, $Qe_0=-\tfrac12d^*de_0$ on $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ and $Qe_0={\not d}e_0$ on $\lambda$, which vanish exactly for the three kinds of $e_0$ listed.

For $e\in\mathscr E_c$ the pairing $\langle e_0,e\rangle$ is defined, and integration by parts with compact support gives $\langle e_0,Qe\rangle=-(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle Qe_0,e\rangle=0$, as in Proposition 1.11; so the functional is $Q$-closed.
A $Q$-exact linear functional on $\mathscr E_c$ is, up to sign, $G\circ Q$ for a linear functional $G$.

The operator $Q$ vanishes on the slots of $c^*$, $\lambda^*$ and $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, so $G\circ Q$ is independent of the components of $e$ in these slots, while $\langle e_0,e\rangle$ is the pairing of $e_0$ with the component of $e$ in the partner slot of $e_0$, which is one of these three, and is a nonzero functional of it for $e_0\neq0$.
Hence $\langle e_0,-\rangle$ is $Q$-exact for no $e_0\neq0$.
Since $e_0$ has polynomial components, $\langle e_0,e\rangle$ is a finite combination of moments of $e$; it extends continuously to Schwartz sections and vanishes on moment-free ones.
For $e_0=X$ in the ghost slot, Definition 1.5 gives $\langle X,e\rangle=-\langle e,X\rangle=-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_{c^*},X)$, with $e_{c^*}$ the component of $e$ in the slot of $c^*$.
Polynomial sections of bounded degree form a finite-dimensional space.
The derivation $Q$ of [C07, §6.2] acts on an $n$-linear graded-symmetric functional $F$ of parity $|F|$ by
QF=(-1)^{|F|}\,F\circ\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\Big),

the operator in brackets being the tensor-product differential of [C07, §6.2], with the Koszul rule for odd operators on tensor factors: in $F(e+rQe,\dots)$ with $e$ even and $r$ an odd element of an auxiliary nilpotent ring [C07, Lemma 6.4.1, proof], the element $r$ passes through $F$.
Corollary 3.20 (Functionals at scale $\infty$).
Let $n\ge1$ and let $F$ be a continuous graded-symmetric $n$-linear functional on moment-free Schwartz sections with $F\circ\big(\sum_{j=1}^n1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\big)=0$.
Then
F=\Big(F\circ\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}\Big)\circ\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\Big),

and the functional $F\circ\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}$ is continuous, graded symmetric and of parity $|F|+1$; $F$ equals $(-1)^{|F|+1}$ times $Q$ of it.
Hence the complex of continuous polynomial functionals on moment-free Schwartz sections, without constant term, is acyclic for $Q$: every $Q$-closed functional without constant term is $Q$-exact.
Proof.

By Theorem 3.19, $P(0,\infty)\star$ acts continuously on moment-free Schwartz sections, so the composite functional is continuous; averaging over the $n$ factors keeps it graded symmetric, and $P(0,\infty)\star$ is odd, which gives the parity.

Odd operators acting on different tensor factors anticommute, so the graded commutator of $Q$ on the $j$-th factor with $P(0,\infty)\star$ on the $i$-th factor vanishes for $i\neq j$, and for $i=j$ it is the identity of the $i$-th factor by (3.4).

Summing over $i,j$ and dividing by $n$, the graded commutator of the tensor-product differential with the averaged operator $\frac1n\sum_i1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}$ is $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}$.

Composing with $F$ and using $F\circ\big(\sum_j1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\big)=0$ gives the displayed identity, and the action of $Q$ on functionals of parity $|F|+1$ gives the last statement.
Remark 3.21 (Where the content of an operator lies).
At scale $\infty$ the differential on functionals is $d_{CE}+Q$ ($\Delta_\infty=0$, $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$, Definition 3.15).

On moment-free Schwartz sections the cohomology of $Q$ on functionals without constant term is zero (Corollary 3.20): every $Q$-closed functional is $Q$ of a nonlocal functional built with $P(0,\infty)\star$.

On compactly supported sections $Q$ has nonzero classes, among them the zero-mode classes of Theorem 3.19, the pairings with polynomial zero modes of $Q$, such as $-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c^*,X)$ for a constant ghost $X$.
The list of Theorem 3.19 is a list of examples: the slot of $A|_V$ contributes further classes.

For $a,b\in V$ with $(a,b)=0$ and $a,b$ linearly independent, the one-form $e_0=(a,x)\,(b,-)$ satisfies $d^*e_0=-(a,b)=0$ and $d^*de_0=0$, hence $Qe_0=-\tfrac12d^*de_0=0$, while $de_0=(a,-)\wedge(b,-)\neq0$.

The functional $e\mapsto\langle e_0,e\rangle$ is $Q$-closed; a $Q$-exact linear functional depends on the component of $e$ in the slot of $A^*|_V$ through its image under $d^*$ alone, which vanishes on $d^*\beta$ for every compactly supported two-form $\beta$, while $\langle e_0,d^*\beta\rangle$ is $\pm\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(de_0,\beta)$, nonzero for suitable $\beta$; so this class is nonzero.

The zero-mode classes vanish on moment-free sections, sit at $p=0$, are independent of $\varepsilon$, and are finitely many in each polynomial degree and infinitely many in all; products of them give nonlinear classes.
On moment-free Schwartz sections every $Q$-closed functional without constant term therefore defines the zero class, whatever functional $O(\varepsilon)$ it is obtained from.

The content of an operator is the local functional $O(\varepsilon)$ at the UV end whose flow $O[\infty]$ to scale $\infty$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.3] has an $\varepsilon\to0$ limit; both are defined in Chapter 5.
This requirement fixes the singular part of $O(\varepsilon)$ uniquely; the finite part is the scheme freedom.

Correspondingly, an equation expressing $Q\,O[\infty]$ as the scale-$\infty$ observable of a second local functional has content because that functional is local, and for an operator whose observable is a cocycle, $Q\,O[\infty]=0$ (Remark 5.6), the anomalous dimension is read off in the cohomology of local functionals.
3.5 The graph expansion and the one-loop formula
Proposition 3.22 (Graph expansion).
For $J=\sum_{i\ge0}\hbar^iJ_i$ as in Definition [3.16](#b-00460),
W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\sum_\gamma\hbar^{\,b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v}\,\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,w_\gamma\qquad[\text{C07, §15.4}],

the sum over connected graphs $\gamma$ with legs, with vertex set $V(\gamma)$ and edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5] (these always carry the argument $\gamma$) and first Betti number $b_1(\gamma)=|E(\gamma)|-|V(\gamma)|+1$, each vertex $v$ labelled by a Taylor component of $J_{\deg v}$ (vertices of degree $0$ at least trivalent), each edge by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, each leg by an argument; $|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ counts the automorphisms fixing the legs, and $w_\gamma$ is obtained from the full multilinear vertex functions, contracted along the edges and summed over all component labels.
Edge rule: two contracted coordinate functionals, brought adjacent by Koszul reordering, are replaced by the component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ in the same order (Definition 3.10).
At order $\hbar^1$ either $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and all vertices have degree $0$, or $b_1(\gamma)=0$ and exactly one vertex has degree $1$, for instance a counterterm vertex.
Proof.
Write $\phi=P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\sum\phi^{\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}$.

Expanding the exponentials, a term of $e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}$ is a set of vertices, each a factor $\hbar^{\deg v-1}J_{\deg v}$, with $|E(\gamma)|$ pairs of half-edges contracted by $\hbar\partial_\phi$; the factor $\frac12$ in $\partial_\phi=\frac12\sum\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}$ [C07, §6.4] and the factorials of the exponentials combine to $1/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$, and on two coordinate functionals $\partial_\phi$ returns the component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ in their order.
The logarithm keeps the connected graphs, and the overall factor $\hbar$ gives the power
\hbar^{1+|E(\gamma)|-|V(\gamma)|+\sum_v\deg v}=\hbar^{b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v}.
The last statement is $b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v=1$.

For the one-loop formula let $\mathscr E$ be a finite-dimensional super vector space, as when the manifold of [C07, §6.6, §10.1] is a point, and let $\phi=\sum\phi^{\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$ be even with complex coefficients [C07, §6.4].

Let $J$ be a quadratic functional on $\mathscr E$, even as a whole, whose coefficients lie in a supercommutative algebra: the complex numbers, or an auxiliary nilpotent ring with odd elements as in [C07, Lemma 6.4.1, proof].
The one-loop operator of $(\phi,J)$ is the linear map
e\mapsto\sum\phi^{\prime}\,(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\,\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_eJ ,

i.e. $\phi$ composed with the parity operator $(-1)^{|\cdot|}$ composed with the second derivative of $J$, the right-hand slot differentiated first, with the coefficients written to the right and extended linearly over them.

$\mathrm{STr}$ is the supertrace on such linear maps [CG2, §13.7.2]: on the map $e\mapsto e_0\,\ell(e)$, with $e_0\in\mathscr E$ homogeneous and $\ell$ a linear functional with values in the coefficients, it is $(-1)^{|e_0|}\ell(e_0)$.
Proposition 3.23 (One-loop formula).
As formal power series in $J$,

\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\Big|_{e=0}=\hbar\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{2n}\,\mathrm{STr}\big((\text{one-loop operator})^n\big)=-\frac\hbar2\,\mathrm{STr}\log\big(1-\text{one-loop operator}\big). \tag{3.5}
The term $n=1$ is $\hbar\,\partial_\phi J$, and the term of order $n$ is the sum of the cycles with $n$ vertices, whose automorphism group has order $2n$.
Proof.
Two identities for an even quadratic functional $F$ with coefficients as above.

The second derivative $\partial_e\partial_{e'}F$ is a coefficient of parity $|e|+|e'|$ with $\partial_e\partial_{e'}F=(-1)^{|e||e'|}\partial_{e'}\partial_eF$; since $\phi$ is even, $|\phi^{\prime}|=|\phi^{\prime\prime}|$ in every term.
First, $\tfrac12\mathrm{STr}$ of the one-loop operator of $F$ is $\partial_\phi F$: by the rank-one formula,

\tfrac12\mathrm{STr}=\tfrac12\sum(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime}|+|\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\,\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F=\tfrac12\sum\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F=\partial_\phi F .

Second, since $\partial_\phi$ is of order two, $\partial_\phi(F_1F_2)-(\partial_\phi F_1)F_2-F_1(\partial_\phi F_2)$ is the sum of the two terms with one derivative on each factor; for $F_1$ even, the graded symmetry $\sum\phi^{\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}=\sum(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime}||\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\phi^{\prime\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime}$ makes the two terms equal, so this sum is $\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F_1)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F_2)$.
It is a derivation in each argument; hence, by induction on $m$,
\partial_\phi(F^m)=m\,(\partial_\phi F)\,F^{m-1}+\tfrac12m(m-1)\,F^{m-2}\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F),
\partial_\phi e^{F/\hbar}=e^{F/\hbar}\Big(\hbar^{-1}\partial_\phi F+\tfrac12\hbar^{-2}\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F)\Big).
The one-loop operator of the quadratic functional $\tfrac12\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F)$ is the square of the one-loop operator of $F$.

Indeed, the Leibniz rule for the linear functionals $\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F$ and $\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F$ gives two terms for the second derivative, which coincide after the graded symmetry of $\phi$ and the exchange of the two coefficients, so that

\partial_e\partial_{e'}\Big(\tfrac12\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F)\Big)=\sum(-1)^{|e'||\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\,(\partial_e\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)\,(\partial_{e'}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F).

Writing $\phi=\sum_k\phi^{\prime}_k\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}_k=\sum_l\phi^{\prime}_l\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}_l$ for two copies of the same sum, the one-loop operator of this functional sends $e$ to

\sum_{l,k}\phi^{\prime}_l(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_l|}(-1)^{|e||\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_l}\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}F)(\partial_e\partial_{\phi^{\prime}_k}F)=\sum_{l,k}\phi^{\prime}_l(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_l|}(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_l}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}_k}F)(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}\partial_eF),

where the graded symmetry of $\phi$ in the index $k$ contributes $(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}$ and $\partial_e\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}F=(-1)^{|e||\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}\partial_eF$; the right side is the one-loop operator of $F$ applied twice to $e$.
The flow in an auxiliary formal parameter $s$.
Let $J_s$ be the quadratic functional determined, as a formal power series in $s$ and in $J$, by
\frac{d}{ds}J_s=\tfrac12\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}J_s)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}J_s),\qquad J_0=J .

By the formula for $\partial_\phi e^{F/\hbar}$ with $F=J_s$, the functional $\exp\big(\int_0^s\partial_\phi J_{s^{\prime}}\,ds^{\prime}\big)e^{J_s/\hbar}$ satisfies $\frac{d}{ds}(\cdots)=\hbar\partial_\phi(\cdots)$, as does $e^{s\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}$; both equal $e^{J/\hbar}$ at $s=0$, and this equation determines the coefficient of each power of $s$ from the previous one, so they coincide.
At order $m$ in $J$ the powers $s^k$ that occur have $k\le m$, because $\partial_\phi$ lowers the polynomial degree by two and $J^m$ has degree $2m$; so $s=1$ may be substituted.
At the origin $e^{J_1/\hbar}$ equals $1$, hence
\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\Big|_{e=0}=\hbar\int_0^1\partial_\phi J_s\,ds .

The one-loop operator of $J_s$ depends linearly on $J_s$, so by the second identity its derivative in $s$ is its square; its value at $s=0$ is the one-loop operator of $J$, and the unique formal solution is $\sum_{n\ge1}s^{n-1}(\text{one-loop operator of }J)^n$.
By the first identity,
which is (3.5), with $\mathrm{STr}\log(1-\text{one-loop operator})=-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1n\mathrm{STr}\big((\text{one-loop operator})^n\big)$.
The term $n=1$ is $\hbar\,\partial_\phi J$ by the first identity.
In the graph expansion with vertices $J$ the graphs without legs and with bivalent vertices are the cycles, and a cycle with $n$ vertices has $2n$ automorphisms.
Remark 3.24 (Use in the field theory).

For the one-loop part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I)$ at a background field configuration, $J$ is the part of $I(\text{background}+\text{fluctuation})$ quadratic in the fluctuation, $\phi=P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, $\mathrm{STr}$ includes the trace over $\mathfrak g$ and the integration over positions, and expanding in the background produces the one-loop one-particle-irreducible graphs with their external legs; the parity operator and the supertrace produce the signs of fermion and ghost loops.

When the background contains odd fields, multiplied by odd elements of an auxiliary nilpotent ring as in Definition 1.13, the coefficients of $J$ contain odd elements, and Proposition 3.23 applies with these coefficients.
4. Counterterms at one loop and the quantum master equation at the UV boundary

The one-loop counterterm, the analogue on $\mathbb R^4$ at order $\hbar$ of the counterterm of [C07, Thm B] (Remark 4.9), is fixed by the requirement that the order-$\hbar$ part of the flow $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ have a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta, and it is unique among the translation-invariant and $\mathfrak g$-invariant local functionals with coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ (Propositions 4.8 and 4.10).

The regulator, however, cuts every edge at the Schwinger time $\varepsilon$ and breaks the gauge symmetry, so the one-loop counterterm contains the mass terms $\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$, whose $Q$-variation is nonzero.

Transported to the UV boundary by Theorem 3.17, the quantum master equation then fails by a finite local functional, and a finite local counterterm has to be chosen to remove it: this is the first renormalisation condition of the theory.

This chapter computes $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in every one-loop sector of superficial degree $\ge0$, identifies its $\log\varepsilon$ part as a rescaling of the fields with vanishing component along the coupling, and evaluates the master equation at the UV boundary in the sector with legs $(c,A|_V)$, where the first finite counterterm appears.
4.1 The one-loop counterterm and its boundary form
Throughout this chapter $\mathfrak g$ is simple.

Then the Killing form $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)$ is a multiple of the invariant pairing, and the ratio $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$, for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,Y)\neq0$, is a number independent of $X$ and $Y$.
Every one-loop coefficient of this chapter is a rational multiple of
\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)},
except the coefficients of the fourth-order adjoint traces of the quartic graphs, which are rational multiples of $\hbar/16\pi^2$.
The upper Schwinger limit is $\infty$ (Chapter 3).

The value of a translation-invariant functional with $k$ legs on plane waves $e^{i(p_j,x)}$, $j=1,\dots,k$, with fibre elements as in Definition 1.13, is $(2\pi)^4\delta(p_1+\dots+p_k)$ times a function of $(p_1,\dots,p_k)$ on the subspace where $p_1+\dots+p_k=0$; this function is its plane-wave value.
Leg momenta are generic when every leg momentum is nonzero and no sum of the momenta of a nonempty proper subset of the legs vanishes.
For $k=1$ the set of generic configurations is empty; for $k\ge2$ it is the complement of finitely many proper linear subspaces of the subspace $p_1+\dots+p_k=0$, an open dense subset.

A functional depending on $\varepsilon$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta when the plane-wave values of its Taylor components converge as $\varepsilon\to0$ at every generic configuration of the leg momenta.
Every limit of a flow in this chapter is a limit in this sense.
Definition 4.1 (One-loop counterterm).

For a connected one-particle-irreducible graph $\gamma$ with legs, $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and all vertices labelled by $I$ (Proposition 3.22), let $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ be its value with every edge labelled by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §15.4].

Every vertex of $\gamma$ lies on its cycle and carries a leg, so at generic leg momenta the momenta of distinct edges of $\gamma$ differ, and by Lemma 4.6, as $\varepsilon\to0$, the plane-wave value of $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the sum of multiples of negative integer powers of $\varepsilon$, a multiple of $\log\varepsilon$, and a function of $\varepsilon$ with a limit; the first two are polynomials in the leg momenta, and $\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ denotes the local functional whose plane-wave value is their sum [CG2, §13.7.2].
The one-loop counterterm is
I^{CT}[\varepsilon]=\hbar\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon\,w_\gamma(\varepsilon), \tag{4.1}
the sum over the connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and at least two legs, modulo constants.
Its coefficients lie in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ (Proposition 4.20), the one-loop part of the renormalisation scheme $\mathscr A_{<0}$ [C07, Def 1.4.1; CG2, §13.7.2].
The $\varepsilon$-dependence of a graph is carried by the lower ends of its Schwinger integrals.
By (3.2), $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-L_\varepsilon$ with $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$.
Proposition 4.2 (Boundary form of the scale derivative).
Let $\gamma$ be a graph with edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5], and let $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ be its value with every edge labelled by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$.
Then

\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{e\in E(\gamma)}w_\gamma\big(\text{edge }e\text{ labelled by }-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon,\ \text{the other edges by }P(\varepsilon,\infty)\big). \tag{4.2}

In the Schwinger form $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}f_\gamma\prod_{e}dt_e$ of [C07, §15.5], with the edge $e$ carrying $L_{t_e}$, the $e$-th term of [(4.2)](#b-00563) is
-\varepsilon\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)\setminus\{e\}}}f_\gamma\big|_{t_e=\varepsilon}\prod_{e'\neq e}dt_{e'} .
Proof.
The value $w_\gamma$ is multilinear in the kernels labelling the edges, so the Leibniz rule gives
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma=\sum_e w_\gamma\Big(\text{edge }e\text{ labelled by }\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)\Big),
and $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-L_\varepsilon$ by (3.2).
In the Schwinger form, $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int_\varepsilon^\infty(\cdots)\,dt_e=-(\cdots)|_{t_e=\varepsilon}$ for each edge.
Corollary 4.3 (Singular part from the boundary).
At fixed leg momenta, if the right-hand side of [(4.2)](#b-00563) equals $-a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b$ plus a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$, with $a$, $b$ independent of $\varepsilon$, then

w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b\log\varepsilon+(\text{a function of }\varepsilon\text{ with a limit}),\qquad \mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b\log\varepsilon .
Proof.

$\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(w_\gamma-a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\log\varepsilon\big)=\varepsilon^{-1}\big(\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma+a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\big)$ is $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$, hence bounded near $\varepsilon=0$, so $w_\gamma-a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\log\varepsilon$ has a limit and differs from it by a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$.

For one-loop graphs with at most two edges, the Schwinger integrals reduce to four elementary ones after a Gaussian integral over the loop momentum.
Lemma 4.4 (Gaussian integral over the loop momentum).
Let $t_1,t_2>0$, $p\in V$, and let the numerator be a polynomial function of $p_1\in V$ of degree at most two.
Then
the positive Laplacian, minus the sum of the second derivatives along an orthonormal basis, being taken in the variable $p_1$.
Proof.
Completing the square and integrating the Gaussian,
The normalised Gaussian average in the shifted variable has vanishing odd moments, and its second moment sends $(v,p_1)(v',p_1)$ to $(v,v')/(2(t_1+t_2))$ for $v,v'\in V$.

A polynomial of degree at most two is its value at the centre plus a linear term plus its quadratic part; the average of the quadratic part is $\frac{1}{4(t_1+t_2)}$ times the sum of the second derivatives along an orthonormal basis, i.e. $-\frac{1}{4(t_1+t_2)}$ times the positive Laplacian of the numerator in $p_1$.
Lemma 4.5 (Elementary Schwinger integrals).
For $p\neq0$, modulo functions of $\varepsilon$ with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ ($\mathscr A_{\ge0}$ of [C07, Def 1.4.1]),
Proof.

The integrands are symmetric in $t_1,t_2$, so by Proposition 4.2 each $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ equals $-2\varepsilon$ times the integral over $t\in[\varepsilon,\infty)$ of the integrand at $t_1=\varepsilon$, $t_2=t$.

On the pinned edge the exponent satisfies $0\le\frac{\varepsilon t|p|^2}{\varepsilon+t}\le\varepsilon|p|^2$, so $e^{-\varepsilon t|p|^2/(\varepsilon+t)}$ equals $1-\frac{\varepsilon t|p|^2}{\varepsilon+t}$ plus a remainder between $0$ and $\tfrac12\varepsilon^2|p|^4$, uniformly in $t$.

the three pinned integrals are, up to terms bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$,
Corollary 4.3 with $(a,b)$ equal to $(\tfrac14,\tfrac16|p|^2)$, $(0,-1)$, $(0,-\tfrac16)$ gives the three expansions.
The one-edge integral is exact.
Lemma 4.6 (Singular part of a one-loop graph).
Let $\gamma$ be a connected one-particle-irreducible graph with $b_1(\gamma)=1$, so that every vertex lies on the cycle and $|E(\gamma)|=|V(\gamma)|$.

Let its vertex functions be polynomials in the momenta, up to a factor depending on the leg momenta alone (such as the Fourier transform of a four-form at minus the total leg momentum, Chapter 5), and let its numerator, the product of the vertex functions and of the polynomial factors of the edge components of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (Proposition 3.11), be homogeneous in the loop momentum and the leg momenta; for vertices labelled by $I$ and legs in fixed slots this holds by Lemma 4.18.
Its superficial degree is the degree of the numerator plus $4-2|E(\gamma)|$.
Let the leg momenta be such that the momenta of any two distinct edges differ by a nonzero vector.
Then, at these leg momenta and as $\varepsilon\to0$,
w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{1\le k\le\frac12(\text{superficial degree})}\varepsilon^{-k}\,a_k+b\,\log\varepsilon+(\text{a function of }\varepsilon\text{ with a limit}),

where $a_k$ and $b$ are polynomials in the leg momenta, $a_k$ homogeneous of degree (superficial degree)$-2k$ and $b$ homogeneous of degree equal to the superficial degree, and $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the function with a limit tends to $0$.

In particular the sum of the terms with $\varepsilon^{-k}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ is the plane-wave value of a local functional, $\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$, and it vanishes when the superficial degree is negative.
Proof.
Let the edge $e\in E(\gamma)$ carry the momentum $p_1-q_e$, with $p_1$ the loop momentum and $q_e$ a sum of leg momenta, so that $q_e\neq q_f$ for $e\neq f$.

By Proposition 3.11, $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the integral over $p_1$, with the measure $d^4p_1/(2\pi)^4$, of the numerator times $\prod_ee^{-\varepsilon|p_1-q_e|^2}/|p_1-q_e|^2$, and $e^{-\varepsilon|k|^2}/|k|^2=\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t|k|^2}dt$ introduces a Schwinger time $t_e$ for each edge.
By Tonelli's theorem,

\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}\big|\text{numerator}\big|\,e^{-\sum_et_e|p_1-q_e|^2}\prod_edt_e=\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}\,\big|\text{numerator}\big|\prod_e\frac{e^{-\varepsilon|p_1-q_e|^2}}{|p_1-q_e|^2},

and the right side is finite: the points $p_1=q_e$ are distinct, near each of them exactly one factor is singular, $|p_1-q_e|^{-2}$ being integrable near $p_1=q_e$ in four dimensions, and the Gaussian factors bound the polynomial numerator at large $|p_1|$.

By Fubini's theorem, $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the integral over $t\in[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}$ of the integral over $p_1$, with the measure $\prod_edt_e\,d^4p_1/(2\pi)^4$, of $\exp\big(-\sum_et_e|p_1-q_e|^2\big)$ times the numerator.
Write $\tau=\sum_et_e$.
Completing the square,
\sum_et_e|p_1-q_e|^2=\tau\Big|p_1-\sum_e\frac{t_e}{\tau}\,q_e\Big|^2+\tau\cdot\frac12\sum_{e,f}\frac{t_e}{\tau}\frac{t_f}{\tau}|q_e-q_f|^2 ,
and the Gaussian integral over $p_1$, with the moments of Lemma [4.4](#b-00577) (each contracted pair of loop momenta gives $(2\tau)^{-1}$ times the metric), gives

w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j\ge0}\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}\frac{(\text{numerator})_j}{16\pi^2\,\tau^{2+j}}\,\exp\Big(-\tau\cdot\frac12\sum_{e,f}\frac{t_e}{\tau}\frac{t_f}{\tau}|q_e-q_f|^2\Big)\prod_edt_e ,

where $(\text{numerator})_j$, the part with $j$ contracted pairs, is a polynomial in the ratios $t_e/\tau$ and the leg momenta, homogeneous of degree (degree of the numerator)$-2j$, and zero when $2j$ exceeds the degree of the numerator.
Put $m_j=j+2-|E(\gamma)|$; then $(\text{numerator})_j\neq0$ implies $2m_j\le$ (superficial degree).
The ratios $t_e/\tau$ range over the simplex $\sum_et_e/\tau=1$, and $\prod_edt_e$ is $\tau^{|E(\gamma)|-1}d\tau$ times the Lebesgue measure of the simplex.

Since $\sum_{e\neq f}t_et_f/\tau^2=1-\sum_et_e^2/\tau^2\ge1-\max_et_e/\tau$, the factor multiplying $\tau$ in the exponent is at least one half of the smallest of the numbers $|q_e-q_f|^2$, $e\neq f$, times $1-\max_et_e/\tau$, and $\tau(1-\max_et_e/\tau)$ is the sum of the Schwinger times other than the largest.
The region $\tau\ge1$.
The integrand of the $j$-th term is bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-2-j}$ times the exponential of minus a positive multiple of the sum of the Schwinger times other than the largest.

Integrating these times against the exponential, and the largest time, which is at least $\tau/|E(\gamma)|\ge1/|E(\gamma)|$, against $\tau^{-2-j}$, gives a bound independent of $\varepsilon$; by dominated convergence this part has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$.
The region $\tau\le1$.
If $m_j<0$, the integrand times $\tau^{|E(\gamma)|-1}$ is bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-1-m_j}$, which is integrable, and the part has a limit.
If $m_j\ge0$, expand the exponential to order $m_j$.
The remainder is bounded by $1/(m_j+1)!$ times the $(m_j+1)$-th power of the exponent, so its contribution is bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-2-j+m_j+1}\tau^{|E(\gamma)|-1}=\tau^0$ and has a limit.

The term of order $i\le m_j$ is the integral, over the part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$, of $(16\pi^2\,i!)^{-1}(\text{numerator})_j$ times the $i$-th power of minus the factor multiplying $\tau$ in the exponent, times

\int_{\varepsilon/\min_e(t_e/\tau)}^{1}\tau^{-1-(m_j-i)}\,d\tau=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\varepsilon^{-(m_j-i)}\big(\min_et_e/\tau\big)^{m_j-i}-1}{m_j-i}, & i<m_j,\\[2mm] \log\big(\min_et_e/\tau\big)-\log\varepsilon, & i=m_j.\end{cases}

The part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$ has measure at most a multiple of $\varepsilon$, the function $(\min_et_e/\tau)^{m_j-i}$ is at most $\varepsilon^{m_j-i}$ there, and $\log(\min_et_e/\tau)$ is integrable on the simplex.
Hence the term of order $i

These integrals over the simplex, of polynomials in the ratios and the leg momenta times $(\min_et_e/\tau)^{m_j-i}$, are polynomials in the leg momenta, homogeneous of degree (degree of the numerator)$-2j+2i$, which equals (superficial degree)$-2(m_j-i)$.

Collecting the powers $k=m_j-i$ gives the expansion, with $1\le k\le m_j\le\frac12$(superficial degree); for negative superficial degree every $m_j$ with $(\text{numerator})_j\neq0$ is negative, and the singular part vanishes.
Finally, $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the function with a limit tends to $0$.

That function is the sum, over $j$ and $i$, of the following pieces; in the second and third item the simplex integrand of the term of order $i$ is $(16\pi^2\,i!)^{-1}(\text{numerator})_j$ times the $i$-th power of minus the factor multiplying $\tau$ in the exponent, a polynomial in the ratios and the leg momenta.

• The integrals over $t\in[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}$ restricted to $\tau\ge1$, those restricted to $\tau\le1$ with $m_j<0$, and the remainders of the expansion of the exponential on $\tau\le1$.

By Proposition 4.2, $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of each is minus $\varepsilon$ times its integrals over the faces $t_e=\varepsilon$; by the bounds above these face integrals are bounded on $\tau\ge1$ and bounded by a multiple of $1+|\log\varepsilon|$ on $\tau\le1$, the integrand being at most a multiple of $\tau^{1-|E(\gamma)|}$ there.

• For the term of order $i<m_j$, with $k=m_j-i$: $-k^{-1}\varepsilon^{-k}h(\varepsilon)$, where $h(\varepsilon)$ is the integral of the simplex integrand times $(\min_et_e/\tau)^k$ over the part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$; and $-k^{-1}$ times the integral of the simplex integrand over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$, which comes from the $-1$ in the integral over $\tau$.

• For the term of order $m_j$: $h(\varepsilon)\log\varepsilon$, where $h(\varepsilon)$ is the integral of the simplex integrand over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$; and the integral of the simplex integrand times $\log(\min_et_e/\tau)$ over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$.
The part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau

For a function continuous on the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge s_0$, its integral over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge s$, $s\ge s_0$, is therefore differentiable in $s$, with derivative minus a sum of integrals of the function over the faces where $\min_et_e/\tau=s$, each face having $(|E(\gamma)|-2)$-dimensional measure at most that of a face of the simplex; the same holds, with the opposite sign and $s_0=0$, for the integral of a function continuous on the simplex over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau

In the second item the integrand of $h$ is at most a multiple of $\varepsilon^k$ where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$, so $h(\varepsilon)$ and $\varepsilon\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}$ are bounded by multiples of $\varepsilon^{k+1}$, and $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(\varepsilon^{-k}h(\varepsilon)\big)=-k\varepsilon^{-k}h(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon^{1-k}\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$; $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the integral over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$.

In the third item $h(\varepsilon)$ and $\varepsilon\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}$ are bounded by multiples of $\varepsilon$, so $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(h(\varepsilon)\log\varepsilon\big)=h(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}\log\varepsilon$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|)$; and $\log(\min_et_e/\tau)=\log\varepsilon$ on the faces where $\min_et_e/\tau=\varepsilon$, so $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the integral over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|$.
Every piece has $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ tending to $0$.
Lemma 4.7 (One-loop graphs as trees with a one-loop vertex).

Consider the graphs of Proposition 3.22, with labelled legs, whose vertices are labelled by Taylor components of $I$, except at most one vertex of valence at least $1$, the marked vertex, labelled by a Taylor component of a further functional (in Chapter 5, the operator $O$).

For a connected graph $\Gamma$ with $b_1(\Gamma)=1$, let $\gamma$ be its cycle together with the vertices on the cycle, the remaining half-edges at these vertices being the legs of $\gamma$, and let $T$ be the tree obtained from $\Gamma$ by contracting $\gamma$ to one vertex $s$, whose half-edges are the legs of $\gamma$.
• $\gamma$ is connected and one-particle-irreducible with $b_1(\gamma)=1$.
The automorphisms of $T$ fixing the legs are the identity, and so are those of every tree with the given legs whose vertices are labelled as above except one distinguished vertex $s$.
Restriction to $\gamma$ is a bijection from the automorphisms of $\Gamma$ fixing the legs to the automorphisms of $\gamma$ fixing the legs of $\gamma$.
The value $w_\Gamma$ is $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by the multilinear form $w_\gamma$ in the half-edges of $s$.

• The sum of $w_\Gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|$ over the connected graphs $\Gamma$ with $b_1(\Gamma)=1$ and the given legs equals the sum of $w_T/|\operatorname{Aut}T|=w_T$ over the trees $T$ with the given legs and one vertex $s$, labelled by the Taylor component, with legs the half-edges of $s$, of the sum of $w_\gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ over the connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$.

• A connected one-particle-irreducible graph with $b_1=1$, one leg and all vertices labelled by $I$ is a cubic vertex of $I$ with one edge from the vertex to itself, and its value is $0$ before any integration over positions or momenta.
Proof.
First item.
A connected graph with $b_1=1$ contains exactly one cycle.
Every vertex of $\gamma$ lies on it, so removing an edge of $\gamma$ leaves $\gamma$ connected, and $b_1(\gamma)=|E(\gamma)|-|V(\gamma)|+1=1$.
Contracting the cycle lowers $b_1$ by one, so $T$ is a tree.
Let $T$ be such a tree, with distinguished vertex $s$.
An automorphism $\alpha$ of $T$ fixing the legs preserves the labels of the vertices, so it fixes $s$ and the marked vertex.
For a vertex $v\neq s$, the vertices beyond $v$ are $v$ and the vertices separated from $s$ by $v$.
A vertex beyond $v$ at maximal distance from $s$ has one half-edge towards $s$ and its other half-edges are legs; if it is labelled by $I$ it has at least two legs.
Hence the vertices beyond $v$ carry a leg or include the marked vertex.
Let $v^{\prime}\neq v$ be a second vertex different from $s$, the two being exchanged if $v$ lies beyond $v^{\prime}$.

If $v^{\prime}$ lies beyond $v$ and $v$ is labelled by $I$, then $v$ has, besides its half-edges towards $s$ and towards $v^{\prime}$, a further half-edge, which is a leg or leads to vertices beyond $v$ and not beyond $v^{\prime}$ that carry a leg or include the marked vertex; if $v^{\prime}$ lies beyond $v$ and $v$ is the marked vertex, the vertices beyond $v$ include the marked vertex and those beyond $v^{\prime}$ exclude it; if neither lies beyond the other, the two sets of vertices beyond them are disjoint, and each carries a leg or includes the marked vertex.
In every case $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ differ in the set of legs carried by the vertices beyond them or in whether these include the marked vertex.
Both data are preserved by $\alpha$, so $\alpha$ fixes every vertex.
A tree has no two edges with the same ends and no edge from a vertex to itself, so $\alpha$ fixes every edge, and, with the legs, every half-edge.
An automorphism of $\Gamma$ fixing the legs maps the cycle to itself and therefore induces an automorphism of $T$ fixing the legs, which is the identity.

It fixes every vertex outside the cycle and every half-edge outside the edges of the cycle, the legs of $\gamma$ included, so it restricts to an automorphism of $\gamma$ fixing the legs of $\gamma$, and this restriction determines it.
Conversely, an automorphism of $\gamma$ fixing its legs extends by the identity to an automorphism of $\Gamma$ fixing the legs.
The value $w_\Gamma$ is the contraction of the tensor product of the vertex functions along the edges of $\Gamma$, with the edge rule of Proposition 3.22.

The contractions along different edges commute [C07, §6.4], so contracting the edges of the cycle first gives $w_\gamma$, a multilinear form in the half-edges of $s$, and the remaining contractions give $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by $w_\gamma$.
Second item.

By the first item the half-edges of $s$ are determined by $T$ and its legs, and $\Gamma\mapsto(T,\gamma)$, with the legs of $\gamma$ identified with the half-edges of $s$, is a bijection from the isomorphism classes of connected graphs with $b_1=1$ and the given legs to the pairs consisting of an isomorphism class of trees $T$ with the given legs and a vertex $s$, and an isomorphism class of connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$ whose legs are the half-edges of $s$; the inverse glues $\gamma$ into $T$ in place of $s$.
With $|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|=|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$, $|\operatorname{Aut}T|=1$ and the linearity of $w_T$ in the label of $s$,

\sum_\Gamma\frac{w_\Gamma}{|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|}=\sum_T\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,w_T\big(s\text{ labelled by }w_\gamma\big)=\sum_T\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}T|}\,w_T\Big(s\text{ labelled by }\sum_\gamma\frac{w_\gamma}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\Big).
Third item.
A cycle with $n$ vertices of valence at least three has at least $n$ legs, so one leg forces $n=1$ and a cubic vertex, two of whose slots are joined by the edge.

By Definition 1.13, every cubic vertex function of $I$, namely $A\,A\,A$ (which contains $(A|_V)^3$ and $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$), $\lambda\,\lambda\,A$, $A\,c\,A^*$, $c\,\lambda\,\lambda^*$ and $c\,c\,c^*$, is the form $(X_1,[X_2,X_3])$ in the $\mathfrak g$-factors $X_1,X_2,X_3$ of its three legs, up to sign, times a factor independent of them; by the invariance of $(-,-)$ and the antisymmetry of the bracket, $(X_1,[X_2,X_3])$ is totally antisymmetric.
The $\mathfrak g$-factor of every component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ is a multiple of $(-,-)^{-1}$ (Proposition 3.11), which is symmetric.
The contraction of two arguments of a totally antisymmetric form with a symmetric tensor is $0$, so the vertex with two of its slots joined is the zero functional, before any integration.
Proposition 4.8 (Existence of the limit).
The order-$\hbar$ part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta.
Proof.

By Proposition 3.22 with $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, the order-$\hbar$ part is $\hbar$ times the sum of $w_\Gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|$ over the connected graphs $\Gamma$ with $b_1(\Gamma)=1$ and vertices labelled by $I$, plus $\hbar$ times the sum of $w_T/|\operatorname{Aut}T|$ over the trees $T$ with one vertex $s$ labelled by a Taylor component of $-\hbar^{-1}I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and the other vertices labelled by $I$.

By Lemma 4.7 (without marked vertex), $|\operatorname{Aut}T|=1$ for these trees, and the first sum is the sum over the same trees of $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by the sum of $w_\gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ over the connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$.

A cycle of vertices of valence at least three carries legs, so every such $\gamma$ has legs; those with one leg have value $0$ (Lemma 4.7), and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ has no Taylor component with one leg (Definition 4.1).
By (4.1), the order-$\hbar$ part is therefore $\hbar$ times the sum over the trees $T$ whose vertex $s$ has at least two half-edges of $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by
\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\Big(w_\gamma(\varepsilon)-\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)\Big),
the sum over the $\gamma$ whose legs are the half-edges of $s$.

For a fixed number of legs this sum is finite: a tree with $r$ vertices labelled by $I$ and a vertex $s$ with $m$ half-edges has $r$ edges and at least $3r+m-2r=r+m$ legs, and a cycle with $m$ legs has at most $m$ vertices.
Fix generic leg momenta.

Each edge of $T$ separates $T$ into two parts, and each part carries a leg: in the part without $s$, a vertex at maximal distance from $s$ carries at least two legs; in the part with $s$, the vertex $s$ has, besides the half-edge on the path from $s$ to the edge, a further half-edge, which is a leg or leads to vertices separated from $s$ and from the edge, among which a vertex at maximal distance from $s$ carries at least two legs.

Hence the edge carries the sum of the momenta of a nonempty proper subset of the legs, a nonzero momentum $k$, and its edge factor, a polynomial times $e^{-\varepsilon|k|^2}/|k|^2$ (Proposition 3.11), converges to the polynomial times $|k|^{-2}$.
The half-edges of $s$ carry the sums of the momenta of disjoint nonempty sets of legs, one set for each half-edge.

Two distinct edges of the cycle of $\gamma$ cut it into two arcs, each containing a vertex, and every vertex of $\gamma$ carries a leg of $\gamma$; the momenta of the two edges differ by the sum of the momenta entering $\gamma$ along one arc, the sum of the momenta of a nonempty proper subset of the legs of $T$, which is nonzero.
By Lemma 4.6, with the homogeneity of Lemma 4.18, the plane-wave value of $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)-\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ at these momenta has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$.

The plane-wave value of $w_T$ is the sum, over the components of the internal slots, of the products of the vertex functions of $T$, of its edge factors and of this value, a finite sum of products of functions of $\varepsilon$ with limits.
Remark 4.9 (Relation with Theorem B).

[C07, Thm B] constructs, on a compact manifold with a finite upper scale, a counterterm at all orders in $\hbar$, unique among the local functionals with coefficients in $\mathscr A_{<0}$, for which the flow of the interaction minus the counterterm has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ as a functional; at one loop, its part with $k$ legs is the singular part of the order-$\hbar$, $k$-leg part of the flow of the interaction minus the counterterms with fewer legs, and it is independent of the upper scale [C07, §1.5].

Definition 4.1 and Propositions 4.8 and 4.10 give its analogue on $\mathbb R^4$ with upper scale $\infty$, for the even, local, at least cubic interaction $I$ of (1.3), in the following scope: the order is $\hbar$; the singular parts are computed graph by graph on the one-particle-irreducible graphs, and the one-particle-reducible graphs carry them through their cycles (Lemma 4.7); the limit is the limit of plane-wave values at generic leg momenta; and uniqueness holds among the translation-invariant and $\mathfrak g$-invariant local functionals whose coefficients lie in a space of functions of $\varepsilon$ containing $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ in which every function with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ is zero.
Proposition 4.10 (Uniqueness of the one-loop counterterm).

Let $I^{\prime}$ be a local functional of order $\hbar$, without constant term, invariant under translations and under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$, whose coefficients lie in a space of functions of $\varepsilon$ containing $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ in which every function with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ is zero, for instance the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$, or a complement $\mathscr A_{<0}$ of $\mathscr A_{\ge0}$ containing them [C07, Def 1.4.1].
If the order-$\hbar$ part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{\prime})$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta, then $I^{\prime}=I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$.
Proof.

The vertex functions of $I$ and the components of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ are translation invariant, and their $\mathfrak g$-factors are built from the bracket, $(-,-)$ and $(-,-)^{-1}$; so $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and with it the difference $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-I^{\prime}$, is invariant under translations and under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$, with coefficients in the given space of functions.
A translation-invariant local functional with one leg is, modulo total derivatives, the integral of a constant linear form on the fibre of the bundle of fields.

The fibre is $\mathfrak g$ tensored with a representation of $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ (Chapter 1), so a $\mathfrak g$-invariant linear form on it lies in the tensor product of the invariant linear forms on $\mathfrak g$ with the dual of that representation; the invariant linear forms on $\mathfrak g$ are, through $(-,-)$, the centre of $\mathfrak g$, which is $0$ for $\mathfrak g$ simple.
Hence the difference has no Taylor component with one leg, and by hypothesis none without legs.

The order-$\hbar$ parts of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{\prime})$ and $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ differ by $\hbar$ times the sum of the trees with one vertex labelled by a Taylor component of $\hbar^{-1}(I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-I^{\prime})$ and all other vertices labelled by $I$ (Proposition 3.22).
That vertex has at least two half-edges, so, as in the proof of Proposition 4.8, every edge of such a tree carries a nonzero momentum at generic leg momenta.
By the hypothesis and Proposition 4.8, the sum of the trees has a limit at generic leg momenta.
Suppose the difference is nonzero, and let $k\ge2$ be the smallest number of legs of its nonzero Taylor components.

A tree with $r\ge1$ vertices labelled by $I$, each with at least three half-edges, has $r$ edges, and its vertex labelled by the difference has at least $k$ half-edges, so it has at least $k+3r-2r=k+r$ legs; the $k$-leg part of the sum of the trees is therefore the $k$-leg Taylor component of $\hbar^{-1}(I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-I^{\prime})$ itself, which then has a limit at generic leg momenta.
Its plane-wave value is a finite sum of products of linearly independent coefficient functions of $\varepsilon$ with polynomials in $(p_1,\dots,p_k)$ on the subspace where $p_1+\dots+p_k=0$.
At a generic configuration this sum is a function of $\varepsilon$ in the given space with a limit, hence zero, and by linear independence every polynomial vanishes there.
The generic configurations are dense in the subspace, so the polynomials vanish on it.

A polynomial vanishing on that subspace is a combination of the components of $p_1+\dots+p_k$ with polynomial coefficients, the plane-wave value of a total derivative; so the $k$-leg component is zero, a contradiction.

4.3 Cubic and quartic graphs

The cubic and quartic parts of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ are organised by the Weyl weights of Example 2.13: $A$ has weight $1$, $\lambda$ weight $\tfrac32$, $c$ weight $0$, and the antifields $A^*,\lambda^*,c^*$ the complementary weights $3,\tfrac52,4$, so that each pairing of a field with its antifield has weight $4$.
The weight of a local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\cdots)$ is the sum of the weights of its fields plus the number of its derivatives, and every term of $S$ has weight $4$.

The superficial degree of a graph is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of its legs: $2$ for $(A,A)$, $1$ for $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*)$, $(A|_V,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_V,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, and $0$ for the other cubic and the quartic leg sets below.
Lemma 4.18 (Weights of the singular coefficients).
Let $\gamma$ be a one-loop one-particle-irreducible graph with vertices labelled by $I$.
Its superficial degree in the sense of Lemma 4.6 is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of its legs.

The coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ in its singular part is a local functional of weight $4-2k$, and the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ a local functional of weight $4$; in particular the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ has weight $2$.
Proof.

In momentum space, a vertex with fields of total weight $4-k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ in the momenta, since every term of $S$ has weight $4$; an edge component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ between slots of total weight $2+k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ times $\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t_e|\text{momentum}|^2}dt_e$ (Proposition 3.11: degree $0$ for $A\otimes A$, $1$ for $c\otimes A^*$ and $\lambda\otimes\lambda$).

Each internal half-edge contributes its weight once to a vertex and once to an edge, so, for legs in fixed slots and every assignment of slots to the internal half-edges, the numerator of $\gamma$ is homogeneous of degree $4|V(\gamma)|-2|E(\gamma)|$ minus the sum of the weights of the legs, in the loop momentum $p_1$ and the leg momenta, which is the homogeneity required in Lemma 4.6; with $|E(\gamma)|=|V(\gamma)|$ at one loop, its degree plus $4-2|E(\gamma)|$ is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of the legs.

By Lemma 4.6 the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ is a polynomial in the leg momenta, homogeneous of degree (superficial degree)$-2k$, and that of $\log\varepsilon$ is homogeneous of degree equal to the superficial degree.
The weight of such a local coefficient is the sum of the leg weights, $4-$(superficial degree), plus its degree in the momenta, which gives $4-2k$ and $4$.
Lemma 4.19 (Local functionals of weight at most four).

Let a local functional of degree $0$, without constant term, have weight at most $4$ and be invariant under $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ and the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$.

If it is even, it is a linear combination of: in weight $2$, $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_V,A|_V)$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$; in weight $4$, functionals whose monomials have one of the field contents
In weights $1$ and $3$ there are none.
Proof.
As functionals, $c$ has degree $+1$, $A^*$ and $\lambda^*$ degree $-1$, $c^*$ degree $-2$, and $A,\lambda$ degree $0$ (Chapter 1).
Degree $0$ requires the number of $c$ to equal the number of $A^*$ and $\lambda^*$ plus twice the number of $c^*$, and weight at most $4$ allows at most one antifield.
With $c^*$ (weight $4$): $c\,c\,c^*$.

With $A^*$ (weight $3$): one $c$ and weight at most $1$ more, i.e. $c\,A^*$ with one derivative or $c\,A\,A^*$; invariance pairs $A^*|_V$ with the derivative or with $A|_V$, and $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ with $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$.
With $\lambda^*$ (weight $\tfrac52$): one $c$ and, by $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$, one spinor $\lambda$.
Without antifields there is no $c$; the monomials are built from $A$, $\lambda$ and derivatives, with an even number of spinors.

$\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ admits invariants of an even number of vectors of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ (the invariant volume form of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ needs six) and $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$ of an even number of vector indices from $A|_V$ and the derivatives.

In weight $2$ this leaves $(A|_V)^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$; in weight $4$ the listed contents, a single $A$ with three derivatives being a total derivative; in weight $1$ the single $A$, without invariant; in weight $3$ the contents $A^3$, $A\,A$ with one derivative, $c\,A^*$, each with an odd number of vector indices of $V$ or of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, and $\lambda\lambda$, whose components lie in $S_+\otimes S_-$ (a vector of $V$) or in $W\otimes W$, $W^*\otimes W^*$ (without $SL(4,\mathbb C)$-invariant); all of these have vanishing invariants.
Proposition 4.20 (Structure of the one-loop counterterm).
$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is the sum of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times the mass term of Theorem 4.16 and $\log\varepsilon$ times a local functional of weight $4$ with the field contents of Lemma 4.19.

Its $\log\varepsilon$ part is therefore determined by the one-particle-irreducible one-loop graphs with the leg sets $(A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*|_V)$, the eight cubic sets $(A|_V,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_V,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_V)$, $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,A|_V,A^*|_V)$, $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,\lambda,\lambda^*)$, $(c,c,c^*)$, and the three quartic sets $(A|_V)^4$, $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^4$.
Proof.

By Lemmas 4.6 and 4.18, the singular part of a one-particle-irreducible one-loop graph with vertices labelled by $I$ consists of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ times a local functional of weight $4-2k$, $1\le k\le\frac12(\text{superficial degree})$, and $\log\varepsilon$ times a local functional of weight $4$, and it vanishes when the superficial degree is negative.

The slots of every vertex of $I$ have degrees adding to $0$, and so have the two slots joined by every nonzero component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (Proposition 3.11: $A\otimes A$, $c\otimes A^*|_V$, $A^*|_V\otimes c$, $\lambda\otimes\lambda$); hence the legs of every graph have degrees adding to $0$.

With the degrees of the proof of Lemma 4.19, a set of $n$ legs with degrees adding to $0$ has weight at least $n$: every leg other than $c$ has weight at least $1$, every $c$ has weight $0$ and degree $+1$, and the antifields exceed weight $1$ by $\tfrac32$ per unit of negative degree or more ($A^*$: $3=1+2$, $\lambda^*$: $\tfrac52=1+\tfrac32$, $c^*$: $4=1+\tfrac32\cdot2$), so the weight is at least $n-(\text{number of }c)+\tfrac32(\text{number of }c)\ge n$.
The graphs with one leg have value $0$ (Lemma 4.7).

Hence the superficial degree, $4$ minus the weight of the legs, is at most $2$, and negative for five or more legs; by Lemma 4.6 no power $\varepsilon^{-k}$ with $k\ge2$ occurs, and the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ has weight $2$.

$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is invariant under $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ and the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$ (proof of Theorem 4.16), so by Lemma 4.19 the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ is a combination of the two mass terms, computed in Theorem 4.16, and the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ has the listed contents.
4.3.1 Cubic graphs
Every cubic graph below has vanishing coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$, in accordance with Lemma 4.18.

Its $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient, as a multilinear form in the three legs, is a rational multiple of the tree vertex function of Definition 1.13 with the same legs; the tables give these multiples, in units of $\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$.

The tree vertices are: the $(A|_V)^3$ and $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$ parts of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big(-\tfrac12(dA,\tfrac12[A\wedge A])\big)$; the $A|_V$ and $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ parts of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\tfrac12(\lambda,({\not d}_A-{\not d})\lambda)$; the $A|_V$ and $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ parts of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$; $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)$; $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$.

4.3.2 Quartic graphs

For the quartic sets leg $j\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ carries a decomposable fibre element $(v_j,-)\otimes X_j$ with $X_j\in\mathfrak g$, $v_j\in V$ for a leg $A|_V$ and $v_j\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for a leg $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$; in the set $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$ legs $1,2$ are $A|_V$ and legs $3,4$ are $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$.
A multilinear form is determined by its values on such legs, and by Lemma 4.18 the $\log\varepsilon$ coefficients are independent of the momenta.
They are written in the basis of products of a colour factor and a Lorentz factor:

• colour factors: the pairing $([X_1,X_2],[X_3,X_4])$ of the bracket of the colour elements of legs $1,2$ with the bracket of those of legs $3,4$; the pairing $([X_1,X_4],[X_2,X_3])$; and the averaged trace $\tfrac1{24}\sum_{\text{orderings}}\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2}\mathrm{ad}_{X_3}\mathrm{ad}_{X_4})$, the fourth-order adjoint trace averaged over the $24$ orderings of $X_1,\dots,X_4$.
The third pairing $([X_1,X_3],[X_2,X_4])$ is the sum of the first two, by the Jacobi identity and the invariance of $(-,-)$.
• Lorentz factors: $(v_1,v_2)(v_3,v_4)$, $(v_1,v_3)(v_2,v_4)$, $(v_1,v_4)(v_2,v_3)$, products of metric pairings.
The two bracket pairings carry the unit $\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$, the averaged trace the unit $\hbar/16\pi^2$.
